Read This First
The Promise

I am going to show you the truth about making money online.

Real money. $5,000, $10,000, $20,000 a month, as a beginner, using AI and a method that is actually built on how money works. Not a trend. Not a hack. Not the shiny thing you saw on YouTube last week that will be dead in three months. A method, one you can apply on purpose and get a result, the same way it has worked for my students who started with nothing.

I am against business models. Not because they never work, but because of how they die. The moment a guru puts the best model of the year in front of a million people, a million people run at the same demand, and the thing that made it work is gone. So a model reaches you at the exact moment it stops paying. A method is different. A method finds the opportunity wherever it is hiding this year, and it does not expire when a video goes viral. That is what BDP is, and it is why this book will still work when the models you are watching today are dead.

I am not going to lie to you the way the gurus lied to me. There is no secret button that makes you rich overnight. What there is, is a proven, repeatable method, and a person who has walked the whole road ahead of you, showing you each step. That is what this book is.

Who this book is for

This is for the ambitious. The hardworking. The slightly delusional ones who look at their life right now and refuse to accept that this is it.

And it is for those who are doing it for their current and future families.

If you want to get rich without doing the work, this is not for you, and I say that with respect. But if you are willing to work, and you just needed someone to hand you the real map, you are in exactly the right place.

Everything I got the hard way, three years of failing, $53,000 spent learning, you are about to get a whole lot quicker. Let me show you.

Read This First
How To Read This Book

This book is short on purpose, and built to be used, not just read. Here is how to get the most from it.

Read it in order. The chapters build on each other. The first three get your head right and show you why you are where you are. The next chapters hand you the method itself, pillar by pillar. Do not skip ahead to the tactics before you have the foundation, or the tactics will not stick.

The method has four pillars. Find the Problem, Solve and Package It, Make Them Aware, and Fulfill. Every business you will ever build runs on these four. Once you see them, you cannot unsee them.

Do the Action Steps. At the end of every chapter is a short Action Steps page. That is where the reading turns into money. Reading the chapter and skipping the steps is like reading a recipe and never cooking. Do the steps.

Use the resources. Most chapters point you to a resource in the free community, a prompt, a calculator, a script pack, a tracker. These do the heavy lifting for you. They are already built. Use them.

You will have zero homework left. By the last page, you will know exactly what to do, in what order, with the tools to do it. Then it is on you to go do it. Let us begin.

Chapter One
How I Got Here
I am not special. I just stopped guessing and started following a method. This book is that method.

I am going to show you the truth about making money online.

Real money. $5,000, $10,000, $20,000 a month, as a beginner, using AI and a scientifically proven method. Not a trend. Not a hack. Not the next shiny thing you saw on YouTube last week. A method. One you apply on purpose and get a result.

Everyone lied to me too. For years. So let me show you how I found the truth, by taking you back to the exact moment I learned it.

I have made a full-time income online since I was 19.

Some months, I profit 2 to 3 times what a surgeon makes. I did that before I turned 21. By then, I had also been to more than 23 cities, countries, and islands, in real life, not on a screen. And I flew my parents to Sicily for my mom's birthday, every expense covered.

I am not telling you this to impress you. I am telling you to make you a promise about what is coming, and to earn 5 minutes of your attention. Because none of that is how it started.

It started on a kitchen floor, in Syria, when I was eight years old.

The night my father did not come home

First, you need to know something about my parents, because it explains everything that comes after.

My mom is Christian. My dad is Muslim. Both of their families stood against the marriage, so my parents did the bravest thing I know. They married anyway, moved to a city five hours away from everyone they had ever known, and started from zero. No support. No safety net. Nobody to call when things went wrong. Just two people building a life so their kids could have what they never did. They had been fighting for their place in the world since before I was born.

Then the war came, and it took away even the little they had built.

Like most people, we did not think it would actually reach us. We were wrong. One day, when I was eight, I heard my mom scream into the phone. The call was from the men who had kidnapped my father.

He was gone for two days. Nobody slept. My uncle, the only family we had in the city, came to sit with us, but there was nothing anyone could do except wait. My mom did what she always did. She protected us from it. She sent us to the other rooms when the phone rang. She had already taught us to duck every time we walked past a window, because of the bullets. I remember lying on the kitchen floor, hugging a stuffed Pikachu, waiting for my dad to walk through the door like it was any other night.

The kidnappers wanted money. My dad had managed to save a little over the years, so they released him to go collect it, and they kept his friend behind to make sure he would come back and pay for them both. And he did come back. That is who my father is.

But it was not over. The men came to our house to collect. So we did the only thing a terrified family could think of. We faked that my dad was badly hurt. We put red sauce on his leg and made him look too sick and too broken to ever be worth taking again, hoping they would just take the money and leave him alone. I was eight, watching my family stage an injury in our own living room so the men outside would not take my father twice.

They took the money. From that night on, we slept with a sofa pushed against the door. It could not have stopped anyone, but it made us feel like something stood between us and the world.

That is when my parents decided the war had crossed the line it must never cross. It had touched their kids' home. So they gave up everything they had spent their lives building, the house, the savings that were left, the photos, the friends, all of it, and we packed clothes and nothing else.

The road out

My dad drove. My mom sat in the passenger seat, and the four of us kids squeezed into the back. No seat belts, because in Syria nobody in the back wears one. My oldest brother was fifteen. My sister was ten. I was eight. My little brother was five.

We drove to Hasakah first, to my dad's family, and then on toward Qamishli, because it was the closest city with an airport still open. The war was all around us the whole way. And then one day we took a wrong turn.

The road opened up, big and completely empty, and at the end of it stood three or four tanks blocking everything, with soldiers pointing their guns at our car and screaming that they would shoot. My mom did not scream back. She threw herself over the four of us in the back seat. And my dad, somehow, calmly turned the car around, like he was leaving a parking lot. They let us go. He kept driving.

The plan was to reach the airport in Damascus and fly to Egypt, where we would wait for permission to enter Sweden. My mom's side of the family had lived there for about ten years, and they were helping us come legally. So we waited in Egypt, pretending to be tourists.

And here is the part that breaks me now, as a grown man writing this.

My parents made it feel like a vacation. They took us to the pyramids. We took pictures. We ate out every day. A taxi driver showed us around the city. Four kids, grinning in front of the pyramids, having the time of their lives. And behind the camera stood two people who had just lost their home, their families, their money, and everything they had ever worked for, smiling so their children would not feel any of it.

As a kid, there were even moments I resented them, when their stress spilled over onto us. It took me years to understand what I was actually looking at. They were not two people with problems. They were two people carrying the weight of a war so their kids would only remember the pyramids. I still do not know how they felt in those months. I am not sure I want to.

Then the approval came. We flew, Egypt to Turkey, Turkey to Stockholm. We landed in Sweden on 23 November 2012, into minus 20 degrees, and within days the whole family was sick, our bodies protesting a climate they had never met.

Sweden was not the happy ending

You might think that this is where it gets easy. We thought so too. But we were wrong again.

My grandmother, my mom's mom, took us in. I loved her and I had missed her, and now six of us were living in her little one bedroom apartment. We could not even all fit, so my oldest brother lived at my uncle's place across town. We stayed like that for about eight months until we got a rental apartment. There was a lot of fighting in that time. Not because anyone was bad, but because everyone was breaking a little, in a tiny space, in a country that was not theirs yet.

I am not going to trauma-dump on you, so let me put the next ten years simply. Imagine you, your parents, and your siblings had to fly 5,000 kilometers to a different continent, to a country whose language you did not speak, with no house, no money, and no jobs. At school I was the kid who could not understand anyone, the weird one, left out, at least at the start. Picture what the next decade of that looks like. That was our life now.

It was safer, at least. Tanks in the street are worse than a rough neighborhood, so that was a real win. But being broke does something to you. Sharing one bedroom with three siblings does something to you. Watching your parents sleep on the living room floor for almost a decade, because you cannot afford a bigger place, does something to you.

We moved houses about four times in that decade. My nervous system learned that chaos was normal, and everything calmer felt unsafe. And all I wanted, the only thing, was to make enough money that my family never had to struggle again.

Football was my whole plan

For a long time, I had one plan for that. Football.

I am a Barcelona fan, like everyone in my family. Football was the only thing I knew, and in my head it was the answer. If I go pro, I take everyone with me, we are rich, and the misery ends.

I was good. I played at the highest level a 17 year old could play in Sweden, and I played for AC Milan's academy there too. That meant a 3 hour commute every day, 1.5 hours each way, for 3 years, while keeping straight A's, because in my family school was never optional. I trained 7 to 9 times a week. It was a full-time job on top of a full-time job.

Then, at 18, one question ended it.

I asked myself: if Xavi, Barcelona's head coach at the time, called me right now and offered me a full contract and a starting position, my literal childhood dream, would I take it?

And a voice inside me said no.

I almost turned around to see who had said it. What do you mean, no? It is the dream. It is THE dream. But the voice was mine, and it was honest, and honestly it scared me. Because if football was not the way, then I had no way at all.

What followed was an identity crisis, and probably a depression, though nobody around me would have used that word. But under the crisis, one thing did not move: the goal. My parents. The struggle. I was tired of the misery, and I wanted out fast, for all of us.

And the more I looked at football honestly, the more I saw the trap. Even if I made it, one injury could end everything. One scout having a bad day could end everything. My whole family's future would rest on my knees staying healthy and strangers staying fair. That was too much to hang everyone's life on. So I let the dream die, and I went looking for a new way out.

Three years of doing everything wrong

Here is who I became next: the smartest broke guy you have ever met.

I rented business books from the library. I read financial blogs. I listened to companies' financial reports for fun. I watched hours of YouTube. And I had ideas, endless ideas, all written out in documents. An app for clothes. Wooden dolls to sell to courthouses, so lawyers could demonstrate scenes with them. A plan to study accounting AND law at the same time, so I could one day open the world's first combined accounting and law firm, because, I told myself, nobody has done that.

Notice the pattern. Every idea had to be new. Every idea had to be something nobody had done. Everyone around me kept saying "you're so smart, you're so creative," and I believed them, and I kept planning, and I kept consuming, and every next morning looked exactly like the last one. No money entered my account. I thought I was making progress. I was just making documents.

So let me show you what my "smart" actually produced.

Dropshipping, attempt one. Me and my friends Brian and Daniel sat in Daniel's living room and played a full free YouTube course on dropshipping, pausing after every step, clicking exactly what the guy clicked. It took us about a month to build the website. It took another month just to get approved for payments. We had almost no money, so we put $5 or $10 into ads, because that is what the video said to do. The ads ran. And then our first ever piece of market feedback arrived, a comment from an old lady: this exact product is cheaper at Rusta, the local discount store. We looked it up. She was right. We shut the ads off and never touched the store again. "Maybe this just doesn't work," we said. Remember that sentence. You will meet it again in the next chapter, because that sentence is the cage most people never get out of.

The knives. This one was almost a success story. In Swedish high school, economics students spend year three running a real mini business through a program called UF. My friend found beautiful Japanese-style kitchen knives on Alibaba, so we ordered a small batch and priced them at 5 to 10 times what we paid. We bought red gift packaging from the cheapest store in Sweden. We shot product photos in the school studio. We launched an Instagram and ran a giveaway, and I will be honest with you because this book only works if I am: we faked the winner. We gave the knife to someone we knew and photographed it so the page looked legit. I am not proud of that. I am telling you because you deserve the real story, not the polished one.

And then we actually worked. Our teacher bought a knife. Friends and family bought knives. Our friend Alexander built wooden cutting boards with his dad, and we sold those too. We stood three days at a Christmas market in the cold, plus a stand in the town center, plus one at school. Total result: about $100 profit each, and an A in the class. Real money, made with our own hands.

And the week high school ended, I dropped it completely. Why would anyone drop the one thing that finally worked? Hold that question. The answer is coming, and it is worth more than the knives ever made.

Around those two stories, stack the rest: mini portable fans in the summer. Reselling phones. Day trading, funded by selling some of my own birthday presents to buy stocks. Faceless Instagram pages. Crypto. NFTs. A nightclub promotion business. Two months designing an app I never built, because I am not a coder and never have been. Even a YouTube channel and a gaming dream with Brian, years before. All of it between roughly 18 and 19. Every single one failed or got abandoned.

Here is the part I need you to hear, because it is the whole point of this chapter. None of it failed because I was lazy. I was getting straight A's while training 7 to 9 times a week and studying business on a 3 hour train ride every day. I worked. Hard.

It failed because I was guessing. I thought the way to make money was to invent something nobody had done before, so every time, I started from scratch. New idea, new hope, no proof. I was reinventing the wheel, over and over, and paying for it with years of my life.

Maybe you are there right now, with your own list of tried-and-failed. If so, I am not judging you. I was you.

The weight at home

And I have not even told you the heaviest parts of that decade.

In 2015, three years after we landed, my dad got cancer, and went through a hard surgery. I was a kid watching the strongest man I knew get weak, in a country where we barely spoke the language.

And my mom. My mom would wake up at 5 or 6 in the morning to go to work. She would leave at 3 or 4 and go straight to university, or study from home so she could still take care of us. Then she cooked for four kids, made sure everything was ready for school the next day, and sat back down at the kitchen table to study for hours more, because she refused to be seen as less capable than anyone born in Sweden, and learning Swedish was her quiet insecurity. She is a high achiever, like everyone in my family turned out to be. She never took care of herself. Never had time for herself. Could never afford anything for herself.

There is a sound from those years that breaks my heart to this day. The front door opening. A tired sigh. Heavy steps. Her rushing to her room to change, and then straight to the stove, for us. Her life looked like that for almost five years.

So years later, when I was deep in my three years of failing, those images were burned into me. I sat there with my documents full of ideas and my empty bank account, feeling like a failure who could not help the two people who had given up everything for me.

Then I read one book that started to change it. Rich Dad Poor Dad. It did not hand me a business. It handed me one idea. The broke person says "I can't do this." The rich person asks "how can I do this?" That flipped something. I stopped hunting for reasons it was impossible and started hunting for a way.

The $2,000 bet

A few months before high school ended, I found a Swedish guy on YouTube talking about building a real online business, making $10,000 a month, and how it did not have to be as hard as I was making it. He was running a live virtual event, several hours a day across multiple days, no replays. So I sat in my bedroom and treated it like my life depended on it, because in a way it did. I filled 8 full pages of notes. The date was 23 January 2023. I remember it, because it turned out to be the day everything changed, even though I did not know it yet.

Day one was not about business at all. It was about mindset. They said you have to be willing to learn, that it would be hard, and that your old limiting beliefs would fight you the whole way. Keep that phrase, limiting beliefs. We are going to spend an entire chapter killing yours, because I now know they were right: the beliefs are the real boss fight.

Then they said the sentence I had needed for three years: stop reinventing the wheel. Sell what people already want. They showed the math. If you charge a business owner $1,000 and help him make $10,000, you are not expensive, you are the best deal he ever made. Land ten of those and you have a real business. And then they showed the whole road: how to reach out, what to say, how to book a first call, how to run a second call, how to pitch. It was brief, but for the first time in my life I could see the road instead of guessing at it.

By the last day I felt more hopeless than I had ever felt, and it was the most useful hopelessness of my life. Because it was not "this is impossible." It was "I am done trying alone." I did not want another idea. I wanted someone to show me the way. So I booked the call they offered, got on it, and said exactly that: I want this, how can you help me? They said: $2,000, and we will mentor you and hand you the roadmap.

$2,000 I did not have. I said, "I will ask my parents."

The living room, and the loan

Picture the scene. I walk into the living room and announce: there is this guy, he is Swedish, he is legit, he teaches people to make money online, and he can teach me.

My mom gave me a look I can still see today. The "am I hearing this correctly?" look. My dad actually tried to reason with me: this is a scam, they will take your money, these things do not work. To them it was 95 percent a joke. But here is the thing about my parents, they had watched me grind for two straight years, trying thing after thing, working while everyone else partied. So there was 5 percent of them that could not fully dismiss it. That 5 percent kept the conversation alive.

The answer was still no. And I understood it. We needed every dollar.

So I made my dad an offer, with my older brother backing me up. In Sweden, students receive a monthly support payment called CSN, about $125 to $130 a month, just for studying. Until then, my CSN went straight to my dad, because the family needed it for groceries. My offer: take a loan in your name for the $2,000, and I will pay every bit of it back myself, from my CSN, every month.

I want to be honest about how that felt, then and now. I was asking my family to gamble grocery money on my dream, after three years of me producing nothing. Today I have two little nieces, one of them one year old and the other almost three, and I cannot even say no when they ask to go to the park. So when I think about how many times my parents had to say no to us, to their own kids, for a decade, because there was simply nothing to give, it puts a lump in my throat. That is the weight my dad picked up when he signed that loan. He did not believe in the business. He believed in me.

About that loan, because I know what you are thinking

You have been told your whole life that loans are evil and debt is a trap. Here is what the loan actually looked like: $2,000, over 24 months, applied for online, and the total interest across the entire two years was about $200. That is roughly $92 a month all-in. One invoice a month. That is it. I paid it off early, because the business it bought me started printing money.

Debt for consumption is a trap. Debt that buys you a skill which pays you back is a tool. Learn the difference, and a locked door becomes a door.

The two lessons that built everything

That $2,000 taught me two lessons. They are worth more than everything else I have ever paid for, and this entire book is built on them.

Lesson one. Stop reinventing the wheel

The event hammered it in for days, and then the mentorship made me live it. Everything I had done for three years was backwards. I kept trying to invent something new, the combined law and accounting firm, the courthouse dolls, the novelty. That is the expensive way. The slow way. The broke way.

It is so much easier to walk up to people who are already buying something, and sell them the same thing, done better.

Gym owners are already buying marketing. Someone runs their ads right now. So why not be the person they buy it from? You do not need a new invention. You need a good reason for them to choose you.

You can make your first $100,000 doing what someone else already does, just better. We go deep on exactly how later in this book. For now, kill the "I need an original idea" belief. It is the belief that kept me broke for 3 years.

Lesson two. Focus

Remember the knife business, the one that actually made money, the one I dropped the week school ended? Here is the answer to why.

The course gave me one rule: pick ONE thing, and kill everything else. Not because the knives were bad, but because a person split across five ideas gives each one a fifth of a person. For three years I had been five businesses wide and zero businesses deep. The knives, good as they were, were not the one thing. The agency was. So the knives had to die, the same week they were working. That is what focus costs, and that is why almost nobody has it.

The focus module inside that course did something clever. It did not lecture me, it told stories. Steve Jobs wearing the same outfit every day. Bill Gates, Jeff Bezos, all of them deleting decisions from their lives so the only decisions left were the ones that mattered. I took that as permission. Permission to quit the trading, the crypto, the NFTs, the tiny stock portfolio, the nightclub idea. I deleted the apps. I stopped consuming content completely. From that week on, my only input was my mentors, Samuel and Maksim, and my only output was the work they told me to do.

And I have to be honest about one more thing. They also told me there are only three jobs inside this business: book calls, close calls, and fulfill. Did I listen right away? No. I still burned weeks "researching niches" and polishing documents, because old habits die slow, and I paid for every one of those weeks. You will meet those three jobs again at the very end of this book, because they turned out to be the truest thing anyone ever taught me.

One line from those modules is tattooed on my brain to this day: focus = NOT distracted. That is the whole definition. Not a feeling. Not a morning routine. Just the absence of everything else.

The most successful people I have met are not smarter than you. They are more focused. So how do you get focused? You remove everything else.

Picture a room. White walls, a desk, a pen, and paper. Nothing else. In that room, there is only one thing left to do. Work. Focus is not something you force. Focus is what is left after you delete the distractions.

So delete them, the way I did. Notifications off. Tabs closed. Clutter out. The streaming, the junk food, the endless scroll, the friends who pull you nowhere. Cut them, and what remains is the work. I became the most focused I had ever been, because I finally made it impossible not to be.

The twins in my living room

Now watch how the first client actually happened, because it is a perfect picture of everything this book will teach you.

My older brother is a dentist, and he had just opened a small beauty clinic, Botox and fillers, in a little room of our family's house. One day, two of his clients came over for a treatment: twin brothers who own a Muay Thai gym nearby. They knew my brother well, he trained at their gym, wanted a fight, had referred them a bunch of members. There was trust there already.

So we are sitting in the living room, me being polite because we have guests, and the twins mention, in passing, that they are about to fire their marketing guy.

I froze. I had been thinking about saying something the whole time, and I could not find the guts, because who pitches their guests? And right then my brother says: "Maher is amazing at marketing. He just went through a whole course on it, paid 20,000 crowns for it. He is a pro."

The twins turn to me: "Oh. So you can do our marketing?"

I almost panicked. And then the training kicked in. I asked one question: "How much do you pay your current guy?" They said 5,000 crowns a month. And I heard myself say: "Pay me 6,000, and I will do a better job than him."

They said deal.

The follow-up call was almost comedy. The course had given us a pitch deck template, 60 to 80 slides, and I was marching through every single one, until one of the twins cut me off halfway: "It's okay bro. Just send us the link and let's get started." I pushed for a contract, because that is what serious business people do, right? They laughed it off: "We don't need a contract." We never signed one. I spent the next days convinced they would ghost me.

They did not. I sent my first invoice. 6,000 crowns. About $600.

Six weeks earlier I had been the guy with a folder of imaginary businesses. Now a real business was paying me real money, every month, to solve a real problem. And notice what actually landed the deal. Not my experience, I had none. The twins trusted my brother, so they trusted me. Someone was already buying the exact service. And I only had room to say yes because I had killed everything else. Both lessons, plus one thing you will meet in Chapter 4, all in one living room.

The dinner where nobody clapped

The moment that invoice went out, I started planning a surprise.

I wanted to take the whole family to dinner in Stockholm. Nine people: the six of us, my girlfriend, my brother's girlfriend who is now his wife, my sister's boyfriend. Understand what that meant for us. I had basically never been to a restaurant. McDonald's and Burger King were the ceiling. A real restaurant, in Stockholm, was an event in itself. So there I was, calling restaurants, trying to find one good enough to feel special and cheap enough that nine people could eat on $600, which in Stockholm is a genuine challenge. I even pulled my sister into the secret to help. I pre-ordered starters, shrimp, and a bottle of champagne, so it would all be standing on the table when we walked in. I told everyone: we are going to Stockholm, do not eat before. Everybody dressed up.

And then we sat down, and the moment I had scripted in my head did not come.

Nobody made a toast. Nobody said congratulations. There was no jumping, no clapping, no "we are so proud of you." The evening felt almost fake, like we were all acting in a play nobody had rehearsed. I sat at the head of a table I was paying for, with money from my first client, feeling more pressure than pride.

It took me a long time to understand that night. My family was not cold. My family had spent ten years surviving. When you are born in chaos and raised in chaos, your nervous system learns chaos as home, and it forgets how to do the other thing. How to celebrate. How to be happy out loud. We had all forgotten, together, and honestly, I am still learning it back myself. There is also a simpler layer: I think my parents would still have preferred the safe path for me, the degree, the title, the pension. A dinner paid for by an internet business was not the dream they had written for their son.

I paid for everything, went home, and felt horrible.

So no, my first win did not feel like the movies. I am telling you this because yours might not either, and I do not want that to stop you. Because here is what was true anyway: I was broke again after that dinner, and I was not the same person. The skill was real now. The door was open. And a skill, unlike money, does not run out.

The proof is them, not me

From that first client, the agency grew past $20,000 a month. Along the way I invested $53,000 into my own education. But here is where most people like me lose you. They show off their own results and expect applause.

I do not want applause. I want you to look at the people I have taught, because they are the real proof. A method only counts if it works for normal people with normal lives.

So look.

Angelo. A full-time teacher and a semi-pro footballer, with zero business, sales, or tech experience. He made $3,500 in 87 days after applying the BDP method.

Aman and Mathias. Two partners running one business. One was a pizza delivery driver, the other an electrician. They reached $12,000 a month in 8 months.

Kobe. A high school dropout. He collected $16,000 and signed $50,000 in contracts in 2 months.

Jack Ormonroyd. From $0 to $61,000 in 7 months.

Josh Granger. From $0 to $54,000 in 29 days.

Connor. From $63,000 a month to $130,000 a month in 6 months.

Read those again. A teacher. A pizza driver. An electrician. A dropout. Not geniuses. Not rich kids. Not people with special connections. Regular people who followed a method.

That is the only reason I can promise you anything. Not because I am gifted. Because the system does not care who you are.

Why I actually do this

Let me be honest about why I do this, because it matters.

Universities failed us. Politicians failed us. The online gurus failed us most of all, lying every day, keeping us distracted, making us jump from one thing to the next. When the truth was simple the whole time. Get focused. Pick one thing. Follow a method that is already proven.

And there is the reason underneath the reason. My parents gave up their homes, their families, and everything they had ever built, twice, once for their marriage and once for the war, so that their kids could have a future.

I also had a reason deeper than money, one I had never said out loud until I wrote this. I wanted to make up for everything I could not have as a kid. To prove to myself that I am worth something. Worthy of being loved. Worthy of peace, after a childhood of war and chaos.

Money did not fix all of that on its own. But building something real gave me the freedom to go after it. That is what a working method actually buys you. Not just income. Time. Freedom. The power to take care of the people who took care of you.

You do not get that from guessing. You get it from a system.

What this book is

That system is called BDP. Behavioral Demand Psychology. It is four pillars. Not forty steps. Four.

1. Find the Problem. Find a market that would rather die than not buy.
2. Solve and Package It. Make it ridiculous to say no.
3. Make Them Aware. Make it easy to give you money.
4. Fulfill. Deliver with AI so good they stick forever.

The rest of this book walks you through each pillar, in order, the same way I walk my own clients through it. By the end, you stop guessing. You have a method.

That is the whole promise. I spent 3 years guessing and $53,000 learning, and I put over 120 hours into planning this alone, so that you do not have to pay that price. Everything I got the hard way, you are about to get the fast way.

Let me show you.

Summary

  • The method is what matters, not the person. A refugee kid with no money and no language ran it and it worked, so your starting point is not your problem.
  • Hard work without a method is just expensive motion. Three years of "smart" ideas produced documents, not dollars.
  • The trap was novelty: believing money requires inventing something new. It does not. Sell what people already buy, done better.
  • Focus means killing good things for the one right thing. I dropped a working knife business the week it worked, because the rule is one thing, deep.
  • Borrowed conviction beats solo guessing: a $2,000 mentorship, paid with a loan on my dad's name, ended three years of zeros in six weeks.
  • The first client came through trust that transferred (the twins trusted my brother) and a market that was already buying. Remember that for Chapter 4.
  • Your first win might feel nothing like the movies. Do it anyway. The skill does not run out.
  • The system is BDP: Find the Problem, Solve and Package It, Make Them Aware, Fulfill. The rest of the book hands you each pillar.

title: 2. Why You are Broke
html:
Chapter Two
Why You're Broke
You are not broke because something is wrong with you. You are broke because two systems were built to keep you exactly where you are.

In the last chapter, I showed you how I got here. Now I am going to show you the actual problem. And it is not what you think, because you have been lied to.

First, the three things you should have taken from the last chapter.

One. You do not have to do it alone. Get a mentor, like I did, even if your money situation is not perfect. Two. You do not have to reinvent the wheel. Sell something people already pay for. That is far easier, especially when you do not have millions sitting in a savings account. Three. Get focused. And you get focused by removing distractions.

Good. Now, the actual problem. There are two of them. The first one created the second. Let me show you both.

Problem one. The system that raised you

The first problem is school. University. College. Whatever you call it. It is failing you, and it was designed to.

There is a reason I did not want to study. There is probably a reason you do not either. Look at my situation. I was broke. My family was struggling, and the struggle was mostly about money. We needed money, fast.

So I looked at the respectable path. University. The system that is supposed to be there to help us build a future. And for me it made no sense. First, it would take years. Second, even after those years, I would come out in debt, paying it off, living paycheck to paycheck, maybe saving $500 a month if I was careful. That is not a solution to being broke. That is a slower version of it.

To understand why, you have to know where the system came from. Look up the Prussian system. It is the foundation your school was built on. And the story is wild.

In 1806, Prussia, a German kingdom, lost a brutal war to Napoleon's army. Their leaders sat down and asked the same question over and over. Why did we lose? The answer they landed on was obedience. Their soldiers and their people did not follow orders well enough.

So they built a fix. A compulsory school system, for everyone, starting young. And what did it teach? Not how to think. It taught how to behave.

You sit in rows. You listen to the person at the front. When they walk in, you stand. When they speak, you obey. Step out of line, and you are punished in front of everyone. The whole design had one job: teach young people to obey authority, from an early age.

It was genius, honestly, for its purpose. They wanted obedient soldiers, and they built a machine that produced them.

Then an American came to study it. His name was Horace Mann. He looked at this system and thought, this is perfect for us. So he took it home to the United States and built the American school system on it.

Why? Because America needed workers. The Industrial Revolution had filled the country with factories, and factories need people who show up on time, do as they are told, and do not ask too many questions. The obedient student becomes the obedient worker. It was a perfect fit.

The people in charge loved it. More workers meant bigger businesses, more money, a stronger country. So they poured money in. They funded schools. They funded universities. To produce more workers.

Read that again. The system was never built to make you a free thinker. It was never built to make you rich, or happy. It was built to make you a worker.

And it is the same system today. That is why you were never taught how to make money online. Or sales. Or marketing. Or how buyers actually think. Because a person who knows those things does not need a boss. School taught you there is one right answer and one wrong answer. In life, that is a lie. In business, it is a fatal one.

I can prove it with my own report card. I memorized the capitals of countries I will never visit. Rivers, dates, the works. I can still tell you a few capitals today, and they have made me exactly $0. And in all those years, how many lessons did I get on taxes? Invoices? How to sell? How money actually moves from one person to another? Zero. Not one hour. The system spent years filling my head with answers to questions nobody asks, and not one minute on the questions every adult faces monthly. That is not an accident. That is the design working.

Follow the money: who pays for school, and why

Do not take my word for the design. Run it from first principles, the way you would audit any business: find who pays, then ask what they get for the money.

Who funds schools? The state. Why would a state pour billions into free education? Not charity. An investment. Schools produce workers, workers produce two things the state runs on: labor and taxes. And those taxes flow back and fund the schools that produce the next batch of workers. Look at the loop.

State funds schools. Schools produce workers. Workers produce labor and taxes. Taxes fund the state. Around and around, and the loop is not evil, it is just a machine, and every part of the machine is paid to keep it spinning. Now the question that matters: where in that loop does anyone profit from you starting your own business? Nowhere. A business owner steps outside the loop. Nobody inside it gets paid when you learn sales, pricing, or how to find customers, so nobody inside it teaches you those things. Not a conspiracy of villains. Just incentives, doing what incentives always do.

Once you see it, you stop being angry at school and you stop waiting for it to save you. The machine is not broken. It is doing exactly what it was funded to do. It was just never funded to do anything for you.

How the greatest minds actually learned

So how did people learn before all this? Before the rows and the grades?

They found a master, and they learned from them.

Think about the greatest minds in history. Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor who wrote one of the most famous books ever written, was shaped by his mentors, Rusticus and Fronto, who taught him how to think. Michelangelo learned to paint as an apprentice under a master, then learned to sculpt in the garden of the most powerful family in Florence. Alexander the Great was tutored by Aristotle, who was taught by Plato, who was taught by Socrates.

None of them sat in a row memorizing answers for a grade. They found someone who had already done the thing, and they learned it directly, by doing.

There are no grades in life. Who is grading me right now? Nobody. Nobody can. Grades were built for the factory, not for the real world.

That is how humans learned for thousands of years. You wanted to make a coat? You went to the neighbor who made the best coats, and you learned from him, or you traded him for it. You found the person ahead of you, and you closed the gap. Simple. Human. It worked.

Why the deal broke

Now, maybe you are thinking, so what? Why is any of this my problem, today?

Because of one word. Inflation. Prices keep rising.

The system was not broken two generations ago. Your grandparents may have done fine on it. They got a stable job, they got paid well, and the house was reachable: in the 1960s, a typical American house cost about 2 years of household income. The math worked.

Today that same house costs about 4 years of household income nationally, and measured against a single salary in the big cities where the jobs are, 6 to 8 years or more. Same job, same rows, same obedience, and the prize at the end of it moved out of reach. The deal is broken. So people go looking for another way out.

And that is how the second problem was born.

Problem two. The online lies

Problem two is the online gurus.

You start looking for another way, and they are waiting for you. Let me show you the exact trap, because I fell into it, and I bet you have too.

It starts with motivation. They show you the lifestyle, the car, the freedom. They hand you a shiny new idea and promise you a beautiful future, fast and easy. So you start. You watch the videos. Maybe you buy the course.

Then reality hits. You cannot actually make it work. It is harder than they said, because they sold you easy. So you get discouraged. That part is normal.

Then you do the one thing that keeps you trapped forever. You blame the model, and you switch. "This doesn't work." So you go looking again, get motivated by the next guru, grab the next shiny model, and start the loop over.

I have watched people run this cycle for years. Copy my trading signals and make $10,000 a month, they say. You sit there copying signals, and nothing happens. Just post faceless YouTube videos, they say. You are on your seventh video, nobody is watching, and the only advice is "post more." So you quit and try dropshipping. You learn the website, pick a product, spend money on ads, and then, where is the money? It does not come. So you get discouraged, and you switch again. A service this time, maybe. And around and around you go.

That is the cycle. And here is the trap hidden inside it. It is never actually the model's fault. It is that you never stayed long enough, with a real method, to make any model work.

Follow the money again: how a guru actually gets paid

Run the same audit on the guru that we ran on school, because the loop is uglier and it explains everything you have experienced.

Ask: when does a guru make money? When you succeed with his model? No. He has no idea if you succeeded, and no way to charge you for it. He makes money at exactly one moment: when you buy. The course, the community, the "one last" workshop. That is the entire cash register.

Now play out what that incentive builds. If his money comes from purchases, his real product is not results. It is hope. Fresh hope sells, so there must always be a new model, a new secret, a "this changes everything" video, timed for exactly the moment your last attempt got hard. And here is the darkest part of the math: a student who actually wins stops buying. A student who stays stuck, motivated, and switching buys forever. The cycle you have been living is not a side effect of the guru business. It is the business.

Compare the two loops you now know. School profits from you becoming a worker, so it teaches obedience. Gurus profit from you buying hope, so they sell motivation and switching. Neither loop contains a single person who gets paid when YOU build something real. Which is why this book gives you a method instead of motivation, and why the next chapter starts with you, not with a model.

The two problems feed each other. School failed you, so you went looking for another way. The gurus found you there, they lied to you, and they kept you spinning. Motivated, discouraged, switch. Motivated, discouraged, switch. For years.

The way out

Here is the good news, and it is the whole reason this book exists.

The moment you see the cycle, you can step out of it. There is another way. It is not motivation, and it is not the next shiny model. It is a method. A real one, that works the same way every time, no matter who you are.

I am going to hand you that method in the next chapter. But first, one more thing, because you have earned the right to ask the question this whole chapter trained you to ask.

So what am I building, and how do I get paid?

You just learned to follow the money. So follow mine.

Here is what I am not building. I am not building a coaching business that sells you a course, posts the wins, and quietly disappears when the next trend arrives. You have met those. This chapter is about what they cost you.

I am building a university. The Entrepreneurship University. A real one, for entrepreneurs, where instead of debt and a piece of paper, students leave with a six-figure online business and an entrepreneur degree.

Let me be straight about where that stands today, because this is an anti-guru book and I am not going to sell you a fantasy. We do not have accreditation yet. That is the goal, and it is the direction of everything we build: the degree, the standards, the accreditation, all of it. This book is a move on that road, not the finish line.

Now here is why I am telling you this in the chapter about incentives. Look at the two loops you just learned. School gets paid when you become a worker. The guru gets paid when you buy hope. Both loops pay perfectly whether or not you ever succeed. So run the same audit on mine.

A university is worth exactly what its graduates are worth, and nothing else. Nobody accredits a school whose students fail. Nobody joins one either. Which means the only asset I can build is your result, and the only way I lose is if you do not get one. That is not me being nice. That is my incentive, chained to your outcome, on purpose. Judge me by that standard. Then judge every other person selling you something by it too. Follow the money, always. Even when it leads to me.

Summary

  • You are not broke because you are lazy. Two systems were built to keep you where you are.
  • Problem one is school. It comes from the Prussian obedience system, brought to America by Horace Mann to produce factory workers. It was never designed to make you a free thinker, or rich, or happy.
  • That is why school never taught you sales, marketing, or how to make money. Those skills build people who do not need a boss.
  • The greatest minds learned from mentors, in practice, not from rows and grades. There are no grades in life.
  • The system worked when a house cost 1 to 2 years of salary. Now it costs 6 to 8. The deal is broken, so people go looking for another way.
  • Problem two is the online gurus. The cycle: motivated, you try, you fail, you get discouraged, you blame the model and switch, repeat. It is never the model. You never stayed with a real method.
  • The way out is not motivation or a new model. It is a method. That is the next chapter.
  • And run the same audit on me: I am not building a coaching business, I am building a university where students leave with a business instead of debt. A university is worth what its graduates are worth, so my incentive is chained to your result.
