title: 3. Kill Version One
html:
Chapter Three
Kill Version One
To make $10,000 a month, you first have to become the person who can. This chapter builds that person.

Sunday night, years ago. I am at my desk with a fresh page, and I am writing the perfect plan. Wake up at 6. Train. Work on the business for 4 hours. No phone until lunch. I underline it twice. I go to bed feeling like a new man.

Monday, 6:00 AM. The alarm goes off. I stare at it. Some voice inside says "you barely slept, start tomorrow instead." So I sleep in. Therefore the guilt starts before breakfast. Therefore I "ease into the day" with my phone. Therefore the 4 hours become 40 minutes of half-work. And at 2 in the morning I am still scrolling, telling myself tomorrow will be different.

Tomorrow was not different. Tomorrow was a copy.

I lived that loop for a long time. Every time I got a little closer to my goal, I would sabotage it and slide back into old habits. It felt like an invisible force was making sure I failed. I could not see it, so I could not fight it. Nothing stuck.

Then I found out the force has a name. It is you. The current version of you. And this chapter is where we kill him.

Let me ask you something before we go further. Honestly, right now, what do you think your chances of succeeding at this are? Fifty percent? Ten? Whatever number just came into your head, hold it.

Here is mine, from those years. Zero. Not low. Zero. And I can prove it with my bank statements, because I ran that experiment for three years. Three years of trying things, watching content, waking up ready to change, and my account said the same thing at the end of it as at the start. Version One of me had a zero percent chance, and the evidence was in every month of my life.

The same is true for you, and it is not an insult. If the current version of you could do it, you would already be doing it. You are not stupid, and you are not lazy. You are running a version of yourself that was built for something else.

So the plan is not to try harder as him. It is to build someone else and let him do it.

To make $10,000 a month, you first have to become the person who is able to make $10,000 a month.

Read that line again, because it is the whole chapter. Making your own money, with your own business, is not normal. Most people live normal lives. Normal job, go to work, come home, repeat. You are trying to do something that is not normal. So you cannot stay the normal version of yourself and expect a result that is not normal.

Maybe you are thinking, whoa whoa whoa. I came here to learn how to make money, not to sit in therapy. I get it. I skipped chapters like this too. But here is the thing. I am going to hand you scripts, offers, prompts, and a method in the next chapters. All of it is useless in the hands of the person who cannot wake up when he said he would. I watched people with worse tools than you win because they fixed the person first. So we fix the person first. It is the fastest path to the money, not a detour from it.

The 4 steps to change anything

Forget motivation. Motivation is weather. It comes and goes and you cannot build on it. What you need is a method, and the best one I know is stolen from medicine.

Think about what a doctor does when you walk in. She does not guess. She does not hand you random pills and hope. She runs the same 4 steps, every patient, every time. There are only 4 steps to changing anything in your life, and they are the doctor's steps.

Step 1, diagnose. Where am I right now, honestly? Step 2, outcome. Where do I want to be? Step 3, what is stopping me from getting there? Step 4, the plan of action that closes the gap.

Simple? Yes. Easy? No. Because most people never do step 1 honestly, they dream at step 2 instead of deciding, they blame the wrong thing at step 3, and they never write step 4 down. A doctor who worked like that would lose her license. But that is exactly how most people run their one life.

So let us run the 4 steps on you. Right now. For real.

Step 1: Where are you, honestly?

A doctor cannot treat a patient who lies about the symptoms. So before anything else, we need the truth about where you are.

Let me guess your diagnosis, because I have heard it a few hundred times by now. You are not happy with your financial life. Maybe not with your relationships either, and I do not just mean romantic ones. I mean the friends and people around you. Maybe not with your body, because you "never have time" to train. And your attention is in pieces, because your phone owns it.

How do I know? Because that was my diagnosis, word for word. I was in school, then 3 months of university, not doing much, not happy about any of it. My money situation was bad. My relationship, I self-sabotaged. I was trying to get in shape and I stayed skinny. I would wake up, go to school, try to do some work, and then numb myself with social media.

And here is the sneaky part. I told myself it was not brain rot, because I was watching business content. Podcasts. Gurus. "Educational" videos. I felt productive. I was consuming knowledge every day, and the next day I was identical, and no money entered my account. Consuming is not progress. It is anesthesia that feels like progress.

Have you done that this week? Be honest. Nobody is grading you here.

The 3-question audit

Grab a paper. Answer 3 questions with real answers, not flattering ones.

1. Where is my time going? Not where you plan it to go. Where it actually went yesterday, hour by hour. Write the ugly truth. The 2 hours of shorts count. The "quick check" that ate 40 minutes counts.

2. Where is my energy and focus going? What do you think about in the shower? What do you argue about? Whose drama are you carrying? Focus is a bank account and most people are overdrawn before lunch.

3. Where is my money going? The daily $6 coffee. The energy drink once or twice a day. The nicotine. The alcohol. The going out every other weekend. I am not your dad, and I am not saying never enjoy anything. I am saying name it, because those all cost you money and focus, and you cannot fix what you refuse to see.

Let us make it concrete. Let's say your yesterday looked like this. Woke at 7:40 instead of 6:30, so 70 minutes gone. Phone in bed until 8:15, so 35 more. School or job until 4. Home at 4:40, "resting" on the phone until 6:10, so 90 minutes gone. Dinner, then 2 episodes, so 90 more. At 9:30 you finally open the laptop, tired, and do 45 foggy minutes of "research." Phone in bed from 11 until 1:20, so 140 minutes gone.

Add it up: 70 + 35 + 90 + 90 + 140. That is 425 minutes. Over 7 hours, gone, in one ordinary day. Not to rest. To numbing. Now multiply by 365. That is more than 2,500 hours a year. People build entire businesses in 1,000 focused hours. You are not out of time. Your time is being stolen by the same guy every day, and he lives in your head.

This honest snapshot of you, right now, with the loops and the leaks and the lies, has a name. Call him Version One. V1 for short. Do not hate him. He got you this far. But he cannot take you where you want to go, and by the end of this chapter you will understand exactly why.

Belief break

"But my situation is different. My country, my age, my English, my money." Stop. If your reasons were really the cause, then every single person with your reasons would stay broke forever. They do not. People with your exact starting point, and worse, win every year. I fled a war as a kid and learned the language while other kids learned math. The reasons are real. They are just not the cause. The moment you blame something you cannot control, you lose control. Blame yourself, and suddenly you can fix it. It sounds harsh. But it is actually the best news in this book.

Nobody is coming

Before we look at where you are going, we have to deal with the list. Everybody has one. Mine had ten things on it. Here are the ones I hear most:

  • Wrong country. Wrong city. Wrong economy.
  • Too young, or too old.
  • English is not my first language.
  • No money to start.
  • No connections, nobody in my family did this.
  • No time, I have school or a job.
  • My parents do not support it.
  • I am not technical, I am not a salesperson, I am too shy.

Now here is the question that killed my list. If any of those were really the cause, then every single person who has them would fail. Every one. No exceptions.

And they do not. Somewhere right now there is someone with your exact list, plus a few extras, building the thing you want to build. Aman was delivering pizzas. Mathias was an electrician. Kobe dropped out of high school. Angelo was teaching full time and playing football on the side. They had the list. They just stopped treating it as the cause.

Because that is what a list like that really is: a set of reasons, not causes. They are real. Mine were real. They make it harder. They do not make it impossible, and the difference between those two words is your entire life.

Now the reframe, and I want you to hear it as freedom and not as a beating. Blaming something outside you feels like protection. It is actually surrender. The moment you decide the cause is out there, you have handed the steering wheel to something you cannot reach. You are in the car, you are moving, and you have no control of where it goes. Of course you feel stuck.

Taking the blame is not punishment. It is taking the wheel back. It is the single most useful thing you will ever do, because everything you blame yourself for is something you are allowed to fix. Nobody is coming to fix your list. And once you really get that, you stop waiting, and waiting was the actual thing keeping you where you are.

Step 2: Who is Version Two?

Now the doctor asks the second question. Where do you want to be? Not "what sounds nice." Where are we actually going?

You want to be rich. You want to be free. You want to be strong. You want people around you that you respect and who respect you. That person, the one living that life, is Version Two. V2.

Here is the catch, and it is the whole game. Version One runs from his problems. Version Two runs at them. Version One runs from fear. Version Two uses fear as a compass. Version One lets doubt make his decisions. Version Two hears the doubt and acts anyway. I am not saying this to shame you. I was Version One, and I crossed this gap alone, and it was brutal. You have someone showing you the way. That is the only difference between us.

Make it specific or it does not count

Most people fail step 2 because they answer with a wish. "I want to be successful." "I want financial freedom." Those are horoscopes, not outcomes. Your brain cannot aim at fog.

Here is the test: if you cannot describe a normal Tuesday in your new life, you have a wish, not an outcome.

Let's say two people read this chapter. Person A writes: "I want to make good money online and be free." Person B writes: "In 12 months I collect $10,000 a month from my own service business. I train 4 times a week. I work from a clean desk from 8 to 4, phone in another room. I send my parents money without checking my balance first. On Tuesday I do outreach in the morning, client work after lunch, and I close my laptop at 4 without guilt."

Same dream. But person B's brain now has a target it can check every single day. Did I train? Did I do outreach? Is the phone in the other room? Person A cannot even tell if today moved him closer. Specific outcomes turn every ordinary day into a scoreboard. Vague outcomes turn every day into a mood.

So write Version Two down in 4 areas. Your money: the exact monthly number and what it pays for. Your body: how you train and how you feel walking into a room. Your people: who is around you and who is not anymore. Your mind: what you can focus on, and what no longer owns your attention. Four areas, a few honest lines each. This is not a vision board. This is a target.

Now you have a diagnosis and a destination. A doctor with those two things asks the third question, and this is where almost everyone gets the answer wrong.

Step 3: What is actually stopping you?

You know where you are. You know where you want to be. So what is standing between the two?

Most people answer with a list. No money. No time. No network. No experience. Wrong country, wrong age, wrong economy. I believed my own version of that list for years. And then I noticed something that broke it. People with less money, less time, and worse starting points than me were winning. So the list could not be the real wall. The real wall was one word.

Incongruence · a fancy word for a simple thing: your actions do not match the person you say you want to become. You want V2's life while making V1's decisions.

You say you want a six-pack, but you keep eating chocolate. That does not add up. You say you want to be rich so you can take care of your family, but you are not doing what people who get rich actually do. So what do they do?

They put in the work. They wake up on time, not to post about waking up early, but so they can work on the right things. And let me be very clear about what the right things are not. They are not building another website. Not cleaning your inbox. Not changing your logo color and your business name 7 times. Not texting ChatGPT all afternoon. Not adding a logo to your email signature. Not networking with some guy on social media because he used to be in sales.

None of those put money in your account. Sit in ChatGPT all day, does money appear? No. Polish a website all day, does money appear? No. The right things are the money-making activities. Reaching out. Following up. Getting on calls. Delivering for a client. Everything else is Version One hiding from the work while wearing a work costume.

So the next honest question is: why do you keep choosing the costume over the work? You are not stupid. You know outreach beats logo design. But knowing has never been your problem. Something below the knowing keeps grabbing the wheel. To beat it, you have to see how it was built.

The machine that built you

Everyone has an identity. You might have several. And your V1 identity fights your V2 identity for a brutal reason: an identity wants to survive. We are survival organisms. Our one job, as far as our brain cares, is to not die. So killing an old identity feels, to your brain, like dying. That is why this is hard. Not because you are weak. Because you are built to protect the current you, even when the current you is the problem.

So what builds an identity? Beliefs. And what builds beliefs? Experiences.

Take the belief "I am bad at math." Where did it come from? Your first math class. The teacher yells at you for a wrong answer, in front of everyone. That is the initial experience, and it hurts. Your brain, which just wants to be efficient and safe, files it away and starts collecting proof. Every awkward math class after that gets stamped "see, you are bad at math." Those are confirming experiences, and they stack like bricks. Enough bricks, and you do not have a memory anymore. You have a wall. You have a belief.

Nothing means anything until you decide it does

Take a step further back and something strange shows up. Without a human looking at it, nothing in the world means anything at all.

  • Without a human, $1,000,000 is not a lot of money. It is just a number.
  • Without a human, a phone call is not scary. It is just a phone call.
  • Without a human, the word "no" is not painful. It is just a word.
  • Without a human, starting a business is not risky. It is just starting a business.

Big, small, hard, easy, scary, safe, expensive, cheap: none of those are in the thing. They are in the person looking at it. Which means every drop of fear you feel about this is meaning you added.

And this is the good news hiding in the whole chapter. If you added it, you can change it. The cold call did not get easier for me. I stopped deciding it was terrifying, and the phone stayed exactly the same weight it always was.

Now here is the part almost nobody tells you. "I am bad at math" is not a fact. Who decided? Measured against what? It is a subjective belief wearing a fact costume. Objective means fact: I am holding a pen, there is a desk in front of me. Subjective means opinion: this desk is beautiful. Your identity is built almost entirely out of subjective opinions that got mistaken for facts, because they were installed when you were too young to argue.

So how do you ever break one?

If experiences build the wall, then experiences are the only thing that can take it down. And there are three kinds, not two. You have met the first two already.

  • The initial experience. The first one. The teacher yelling. It starts the belief.
  • Confirming experiences. Every moment after that seems to prove it. They stack the wall higher.
  • Denying experiences. Moments that flatly contradict it. These are the only thing that takes a wall down.

Read that third one again, because it is the mechanism nobody explains. A belief does not die because you argued with it. It dies when it collects enough experiences that say the opposite.

Think about what that means for "I am bad at sales." You cannot think your way out of it. You could write "I am good at sales" on your mirror every morning for a year and the wall would not move one inch, because your brain does not trade in slogans. It trades in evidence. But make 40 calls, and have one person actually listen, and you have created a moment your brain has to file. It does not fit the wall. So the wall cracks.

This is why beginners who take massive action change so fast, and why beginners who only consume never change at all. It has nothing to do with willpower. One group is manufacturing denying experiences every single day. The other is collecting more confirming ones from their bed.

And it tells you exactly what your job is for the next 90 days: go and collect evidence against yourself. That is what Move 4 is for, later in this chapter, and now you know why it works.

And the machine does not stop at identity. It runs all the way to your bank account.

Actions equal outcome. Eat a kilogram of chocolate every day for a year with no training, you get fat. Action, outcome. No negotiation. Business is the same. You take actions, you get an outcome. If you have not liked your outcomes so far, you have been taking the wrong actions. And what chooses your actions? Your identity. And what built your identity? Beliefs. And what built those? Experiences. Experiences, beliefs, identity, actions, outcome. That is the whole machine. Which means if you want a different outcome, you do not start at the outcome. You start at the other end of the chain.

So where do experiences even come from?

If beliefs are built from experiences, the next question decides everything: where do the experiences come from?

You were born with none of them. No opinions about money, no view of yourself, nothing. A newborn does not believe it is bad at math. Everything you believe today got installed later, and it got installed by one thing: your environment. Meaning everything you come into contact with. The people around you, the rooms you sat in, the conversations you overheard, the things you watched.

And here is the part I need you to sit with, because it is the most important sentence in this chapter for someone your age.

Your phone is your environment. Your brain does not have a separate folder for "real life" and "screen." An hour of watching people on a screen is an hour of experience, filed exactly like an hour spent with those people in a room. The videos you watched last night were not entertainment. They were experiences, and they were stacking bricks.

Which changes what the scroll actually costs you. Earlier we did the math and found 425 minutes a day being taken. That is the time cost, and it is brutal enough. But this is worse: those hours are not just stealing your day, they are building the person who wakes up tomorrow. Every video is a small vote for a belief. Watch enough people saying the economy is rigged and nothing works, and you will "just happen" to believe it, and you will never know where it came from.

So do the same audit you did on your time, but on your inputs. Open the app. Scroll your feed for two minutes and ask one question about each account: is this installing something in me that Version Two needs? Unfollow accordingly. Not because those people are bad, but because you only get one set of bricks and you are not going to hand the delivery to strangers.

Then fill the gap on purpose. Follow the people doing the thing you want to do. Read the books. Sit near the ones who are ahead of you. You cannot stop your environment from building you. That part is automatic. You can only choose what it is building with.

The beliefs that were choosing your bank balance

Let me show you the machine running on money, because this is where it robbed me personally.

Growing up, I was handed these beliefs, free of charge: rich people are evil. Money is evil. Money does not grow on trees. You need money to make money. Nobody sat me down and taught them like a class. They were just in the air. Said at kitchen tables, repeated on TV, sighed after bills.

And I believed every one of them, bro. Every single one. Here is what those beliefs did: they did not just slow me down. They stopped me from even looking at opportunities. Why would you study a game you believe is evil and rigged? You would not. So I did not. The beliefs decided before I ever got a vote.

Every one of them was false. Rich people are evil? I have money now, and I did not become evil. Money is evil? Money paid for my mom's birthday trip to Sicily, every expense covered. That did not feel evil. You need money to make money? I started in debt. Literal debt, with a loan in my dad's name. The beliefs were not protecting me. They were keeping me broke and calling it wisdom.

So how did they break? Books. Reading was my first set of new experiences, proof from people who had actually done it. The first one was Rich Dad Poor Dad. And I will give it to you with the same warning I give my students: the author has said some questionable things over the years and has been publicly called out, so be careful how much of him you follow. But the core question of that book, what the rich teach their kids about money that the broke do not, that question is gold. It cracked my wall.

Do not listen to people who are not where you want to be. Listen to those who are.

That principle changed my life, so read it twice. I love my parents forever. They crossed a war for me. And I take zero business or money advice from them, because they never built a business and they are not rich. That is not disrespect. That is sanity. You would not take swimming lessons from someone who has never touched water. So no money advice from someone broke. No relationship advice from someone who has never kept one. Love people fully, and choose your teachers by their results.

Who gave you your money beliefs? Picture their face. Now answer honestly: are they where you want to be? If not, why are their sentences still running your decisions?

The two fears underneath everything

Under the beliefs live two fears, and you need to meet both, because in Chapter 7 you will watch them kill your prospects' decisions too.

Prospect = a person who might buy from you. Someone you are talking to about your service, who has not paid yet.

Fear of failure is not really fear of the event. Nobody is scared of an email bouncing. You are scared of what failure would mean: "it will prove the doubters right, it will prove I am not enough." That meaning is just another subjective belief, installed by old experiences, wearing a fact costume.

Fear of success is the sneaky one. Some part of you is scared it might actually work. Because then you would have to keep it up. Then people might expect things. Then you might outgrow friends, and lose the comfortable story of "one day." So that part quietly sabotages, and you call it laziness. It is not laziness. It is an identity defending its life.

Both fears freeze the same muscle: action. And both die the same way, which is the plan we are about to build. You do not argue with fear. You out-act it, one small piece of proof at a time.

The sides you picked and called personality

One more thing is stopping you, and it hides in plain sight. Years ago, without noticing, you picked sides. "I am not a salesperson." "I am not a camera person." "I am the quiet one." "I am not a numbers guy." You picked a side, filed it under personality, and locked the door.

Here is the trap. The goal you wrote in step 2 does not care about your sides. Building a business will require you to sell, to speak, to post, to count. And every time the goal asks for the other side, your identity throws the veto: "that is not me." Not true. It is not V1. Version Two gets to pick new sides, because the sides were never facts. They were bricks.

And when you genuinely cannot see the right move, use this pocket tool: flip the question. Do not ask "what is the right thing to do?" Ask "what would guarantee failure?" Easy: stay invisible, never follow up, take advice from broke people, quit at the first no. Now do the opposite of that list. When right is foggy, wrong is usually obvious. Invert it.

People do not have business problems. They have personal problems that show up in their business.

Sit with that before we get to the plan, because it explains why this chapter exists at all. The client you did not call was avoidance you had already practised somewhere else. The price you were scared to say out loud was not a pricing problem, it was what you believe you are worth. A business gets built on top of your life, and the weight of it finds every crack you already had. So we fix the cracks first.

Why you build yourself up and then tear it all down

There is one more pattern you need to see before we get to the plan, because you have lived it a hundred times and nobody has ever named it for you.

Your progress is not a line. It is a wave. You get going, you string together good weeks, things start working, and then something in you quietly takes it all apart and you slide back to where you started. Then you climb again. Then you slide again.

Most people think that slide is random, or that it means something is wrong with them. It is not random. It runs on a loop, and the loop is the same every time:

  • Anger. You are in a rut, you hate it, and eventually you get angry enough to move.
  • Drive. The anger turns into fuel. You wake up early, you train, you do the outreach.
  • Pride. It starts working, and you feel good about yourself. Rightly so.
  • Comfort. And pride, quietly, turns into comfort. Comfort is where you stop doing the things that got you there.

Then you slide, the rut comes back, and the rut makes you angry, and around it goes. Look at your own last two years and tell me that is not exactly what happened.

Now the part that actually breaks it, and this took me an embarrassingly long time to see.

Everyone tries to raise their ceiling. The answer is to raise your floor.

You are not your best week. You are not your worst week either. You are the average of the two, and that average is what your life actually looks like. So when you decide to change, you go straight for a bigger peak: the perfect 6 AM routine, the 200-message day, the total transformation. And your peaks were never the problem. How far you fall is the problem.

Here is the comparison that made it real for me. Two people. One does 200 outreaches on a good day and zero for the next nine days. The other does 20 every day, on his best day and his worst. Over a month the second guy does more, learns more, and has a business. And the first guy is exhausted, because every climb starts from the ground.

So do not ask "how big can my best day be?" Ask "how good can my worst day be?" Set a floor so low you cannot fail: one message, one call, one line in the wins doc. Then never, ever go below it, no matter what kind of day you had. Every month, lift the floor slightly. Your ceiling looks after itself. Your floor is the only number that decides your life.

And one warning about the top of the wave, because it is where the damage happens: the most dangerous moment is right after a win. The day the client says yes is the day the devil says "you have earned a break." That is not a reward. That is the slide beginning. Do the outreach on the good day too, especially on the good day. That is how the wave stops owning you.

Step 4: The plan. Kill Version One.

Here is the entire plan of action. Kill Version One. That is it. There is nothing else.

You will never make $10,000 a month online while acting as Version One. It is impossible. You know how I know? Because if it were possible as Version One, you would already be doing it. Einstein supposedly said the definition of insanity is doing the same thing and expecting a different result. Same money habits, same stolen focus, same 2 AM scroll, and somehow a real business appears? It will not.

And it is not that you do not know this. So why is it still so hard to take the right actions? Because you have fed Version One for years. He is huge. Version Two is a baby. Watch how that plays out on an ordinary morning.

Picture it. You told yourself that today you make your cold calls, a real block of them, 2 focused hours pitching your service. On one shoulder sits a devil. That is Version One. On the other sits an angel. That is Version Two.

The devil is a master, because he has trained on you for years. He knows your buttons, because he installed them. "Maybe sleep a bit more, you are tired." "Are you not hungry? Eat first." "If you call now, people will yell at you." "Have you even researched enough? Do you even know exactly what to say?" And the angel? The angel whispers "please, just do it." That is all he has. You have starved him so long he can barely speak.

The one you feed is the one that grows.

So far the devil has won on autopilot. Now we take the wins back on purpose. Here are the 6 moves. Do them in order. None of them need money. All of them need honesty.

Move 1. Drag every belief into the light

Write down every negative belief you hold about money, success, business, and yourself. Paper or a doc, does not matter. Do not stop before 30. The big ones hide behind the small ones, so keep digging. If you get stuck, use this trick from my own playbook: ask ChatGPT "what negative beliefs might a beginner trying to make money online have?" Read the list, and keep every line that stings. The sting is the tell. A belief that stings is a belief that is live.

Move 2. Find the crime scene

Next to each belief, write where it started. Who said it first? What happened? The yelling teacher. The kitchen-table sigh. The cousin who laughed. This step matters because a belief with a visible origin stops feeling like a law of physics and starts feeling like what it is: one bad moment that got promoted way above its rank. Then ask the killer question about the source: was that person where I want to be? Almost always, no. You have been taking orders from people who never made the trip.

Move 3. Demolish and replace

Now run the courtroom. For each belief, write the evidence against it. "Money is evil": then why did it fund the hospital that saved someone you love? "I am bad at sales": measured when, by whom, after how many reps? Then paste your full list into ChatGPT and tell it: "Write me the exact opposite of each of these." Now you hold your new set of beliefs, the ones that lead to the right actions. Save them. Pin them over your desk. Read them every single day.

And before you roll your eyes: this is not affirmation fluff. You are not chanting to the universe. You are reminding a biased brain of the actual evidence. I am good at making money online. Money is good, it lets my family live well. Marketing is good, it brings my service to people who need it. Sales is a skill, and skills are learned. Boring, factual, daily. That is how walls come down.

Move 4. Build the evidence bank

Here is the piece most people miss, and it is the engine of the whole chapter. Reading new beliefs starts the fight. Only new experiences win it. Remember the machine: beliefs are built from stacked experiences. So you are going to stack them on purpose.

Every day, manufacture one small piece of proof that Version Two exists. Made your first call, even shaking? Evidence. Sent 20 outreach messages? Evidence. Woke up at the time you promised? Evidence. Open a doc called Wins and write each one down with the date. One line is enough.

Why write them? Because your brain believes receipts, not speeches. On the bad days, and they are coming, the devil will say "you never follow through." You will open the doc and read 34 dated lines that say otherwise. You cannot think your way into a new identity. You can only act your way in, and keep the receipts.

Move 5. Install the operating system

Now we make the right actions easier and the wrong ones harder, every single day. Three installations.

First, lower your dopamine average. You need to become someone who can sit through a long day of real work without getting pulled away. Distraction is not a character flaw. It is a dopamine problem.

Dopamine · the brain chemical that makes things feel rewarding. Phones, sugar, and games spike it for free. Real work barely moves it. Your brain compares everything to your daily average.

Here is the idea. Everything that gives you less dopamine than your daily average feels boring, even painful. So the higher your average, the more it takes just to feel okay, and the harder it is to sit and do important, boring work. The best entrepreneurs keep their average low. That is why they can talk to a camera or grind a task list for 7 hours straight. It is not superhuman focus. It is fewer competing fireworks.

So lower your standard. This is not "kill all joy." Go enjoy the birthday. It is about not living at level 100. If you want the aggressive reset, here it is: for 24 hours, do almost nothing. You may walk, read, write, and breathe. No phone, no screens, no people, no movies. Drink water, eat simple if you must. You will be bored out of your mind, and that is the point, because the next day, normal work feels fine again.

And protect your mornings like money. Never start your day at level 100. Do not open your eyes and scroll, because then nothing else all day can compete. Start every day with the worst task first, usually the calls or the outreach, and save the fun for the end. Run it backwards and your brain fights you until midnight, hunting for fireworks.

Second, and this one surprised me: fix the small stuff that has nothing to do with business. Your brain does not have a "work mode" and a "life mode." It has one setting, whichever one it runs most often. So every time you quit the last set at the gym, hit snooze, leave the dishes, or abandon a book at chapter three, you are running a rep. You are teaching your brain that stopping when it gets boring is what you do here.

Then at 6pm, when the outreach gets boring, your brain reaches for the setting it knows best. It does not know that this one is important. How you do one thing is how you do everything.

The good news is that it runs both ways, and it is the cheapest win in this chapter. Fix one area on purpose, any area, and it leaks into the others for free. Finish the set. Make the bed. Finish the book. None of those make you money, and all of them are sales training.

Second, live minimal. Keep your space clean. Desk, room, shelf. There is no magic line from "tidy desk" to "money." But clothes on the chair and 5 random things on the desk pull your focus, mine and yours. Simple space, fewer open loops, more focus for what pays.

Third, use the devil-test. The moment the devil tells you to avoid something you know you should do, do more of it. He says skip the calls? Add 10. He says post tomorrow? Post twice today. Every time you do this, you prove to him, with evidence, that he does not decide anymore. He shrinks. The angel grows. That is not poetry. That is the belief machine, running in your favor for once.

Pro tip

Decide the night before, never in the moment. Version One wins negotiations held at 6 AM, because at 6 AM you are tired and he is loud. So close the debate the evening before: write tomorrow's 3 money-making actions on paper, first task on top. In the morning there is nothing to discuss. You are not deciding. You are just executing a decision a smarter version of you already made.

Say this to yourself · the 6 AM script

When the alarm rings and the devil starts his pitch, say this, out loud if you have to:

"I hear you. We are doing it anyway."

Then one question: "Which version does this feed?" If the answer is Version One, do the opposite. Stand up before the debate can start. Ten seconds of stupid courage beats an hour of clever excuses.

What are you actually willing to give up?

Everybody says they want it. Here is how you find out if it is true, and it takes about two minutes.

Write down the three things you are not willing to give up for this. Be honest, nobody sees this. The nights out. The game. The show you watch every evening. The two hours of scrolling. The friends who are going nowhere. Whatever is really on your list.

Now look at it, because that list is the diagnosis. The thing you refuse to give up is your real priority. Not the one you talk about, the one you actually live. And if the things on that list are not building the business, then they are building the version of you who stays exactly where he is.

But read the next part carefully, because this is where every guru gets it wrong and where I want you to hear me clearly. Sacrifice the numbing. Protect the people.

Give up the scrolling, the drinking-because-it-is-Friday, the shows, the pointless hours. Do not give up your family, your training, your sleep, or your closest friends. I did that for a while and it cost me things I cannot buy back, and Chapter 9 is where I tell you exactly what it cost. Cutting the people is not discipline. It is just a different way of losing.

Move 6. Write the one-page Version Two document

Last move. Take everything from this chapter and put it on one page. Who Version Two is, in the 4 areas. The new beliefs. The daily non-negotiables. And one short paragraph most people skip: the shadow. What your life looks like in 5 years if Version One stays in charge. Same room, same scroll, same "one day," just older. Read the page every morning. The vision pulls you. The shadow pushes you. You want both hands on you.

One rule about that page: print it. Physically, on paper, on the wall where you work. Not a note in your phone, because your phone is where the enemy lives, and nothing you put in there ever gets read twice. Same with your new beliefs and your daily non-negotiables. Print them, stick them up, and let them be part of the room you sit in every day. It costs you ten minutes and one sheet of paper, and it turns everything in this chapter from a thing you did once into part of your environment.

And if you want the shadow in numbers, here is the math of waiting. Let's say Version Two, once built, earns $10,000 a month. Every year you keep feeding Version One instead costs you 12 x $10,000. That is $120,000. Gone. Not counting the skills that did not compound, the proof you did not collect, the people you did not meet. Scrolling is not free. It is the most expensive thing you own.

This is going to hurt, and I would rather you hear it from me

Every other person selling you something online will tell you this is easy, fast, and automated. I am not going to do that, because the lie is what breaks people.

The gap between who you are now and who you need to become is not empty. It is full. Full of awkward calls, ignored messages, boring days, doubt at 11pm, and people politely telling you no. You cannot go around that, and there is no tool, prompt, or shortcut that removes it. The only way to the other side is straight through the middle.

Here is the part that matters, and it is why I am telling you now instead of letting you find out: most people do not quit because it is hard. They quit because it was hard and nobody told them it would be. They assumed pain meant they were doing it wrong. So the first time it hurt, they took it as a sign to stop, and stopping felt sensible.

So let me take that exit away from you. The discomfort is not a warning light. It is the toll. It shows up for everyone, including me, including every person whose results you have read in this book, and it shows up again at every new level. When it arrives, it does not mean you picked the wrong thing. It means you are exactly where you are supposed to be, doing the part that most people go home to avoid.

You are going to feel it in about a week. Now you know what it is.

"What if I slip back?"

You will. Let me kill the surprise now so it cannot kill your run later. Somewhere between day 4 and day 11, the excitement wears off. The calls get boring. The wins doc feels silly. The devil switches scripts from "you cannot do it" to "you do not feel like it today." The dip is not a sign the method stopped working. The dip is the method working. It is your old identity making its last real counterattack.

The rule for the dip is simple: shrink the day, never skip the day. Cannot do 2 hours? Do 20 minutes. Cannot do 20? Send one message and write one line in the wins doc. Keep the chain alive at any size, because the belief you are actually building is "I do what I said." Miss once, fine, human. Never miss twice. Version One is not killed in one dramatic battle. He starves, one kept promise at a time.

I built the machine for you

Everything in this chapter works with a pen and paper. And, because I know most people read exercises and do zero of them, I built the whole thing into a guided tool: the Life Design App. It walks you through 7 stages, in order, and does the heavy lifting with you:

Stage 1, uncover your limiting beliefs. Stage 2, trace each one to the moment it started. Stage 3, demolish them with evidence and reframes. Stage 4, build your becoming self across the 4 areas. Stage 5, write the vision and the shadow. Stage 6, install your daily non-negotiables as an operating system. Stage 7, get the final document, your one page, built from your own answers.

The chapter you just read is the why. The app is the do. Do not read about surgery and skip the operation.

Summary

  • To make the money, first become the person who can. You cannot stay Version One and collect a Version Two result.
  • Run the doctor's 4 steps on your life: diagnose honestly, define the outcome specifically, find what is really stopping you, then execute the plan.
  • The audit has 3 questions: where is my time going, where is my focus going, where is my money going. Consuming content is not progress.
  • If you cannot describe a Tuesday in the new life, you have a wish, not an outcome. Write Version Two in 4 areas: money, body, people, mind.
  • The machine is: experiences build beliefs, beliefs build identity, identity chooses actions, actions equal outcome. Change starts at experiences, not at outcomes.
  • Beliefs die from denying experiences, not from arguments. Go collect evidence against yourself.
  • Your environment builds you, and your phone is part of your environment. Audit your feed like you audit your day.
  • Nobody is coming. Your reasons are real, but they are not the cause, or everyone who has them would fail. Taking the blame is taking the wheel back.
  • Your progress is a wave: anger, drive, pride, comfort, slide. Stop chasing a higher ceiling and raise your floor. The most dangerous day is the day after a win.
  • How you do one thing is how you do everything. Fix one small area and it leaks into the rest.
  • Sacrifice the numbing, protect the people. What you refuse to give up is your real priority.
  • It is going to hurt, and that is the toll, not a warning light. Most people quit because nobody told them.
  • Your money beliefs were installed by people who are not where you want to be. Do not listen to people who are not where you want to be. Listen to those who are.
  • Kill Version One with the 6 moves: list the beliefs, find their origins, demolish and replace them, build the evidence bank, install the operating system, write the one-page document.
  • The dip between day 4 and 11 is normal. Shrink the day, never skip the day. Never miss twice.
Chapter Three
Your Action Steps
1
Register for the Life Design App in the community, today, while this chapter is fresh.
2
Complete all 7 stages in one sitting. Block 1 to 2 hours, phone in another room, and finish it today. This is not homework to spread across a week. Do it once, properly, and you walk away with your document.
3
Post your biggest belief shift in the community. The one that stung most when you found it, and what replaced it. Saying it in public is itself a new experience for the evidence bank.
4
Activate the Freedom System inside the app: financial, time, and attention. That becomes your daily operating system from here on.

title: 4. Problems = Money
html:
Chapter Four
Problems = Money
All the money in the world is made by solving a problem someone trusts you to solve. That is the whole game.

The night that first $600 landed in my account, I sat there staring at it, and one question would not leave me alone. How did a broke beginner with no skills just make money? I turned it over and over. And then it landed, so simple it almost felt stupid.

Someone trusted me with their money to solve their problem.

That was the entire answer. He paid me because he trusted I would actually fix his problem. If he did not trust me, why would he ever hand me money? And once I saw it, I saw it everywhere. You make money by solving problems. That is how every dollar on earth is generated. A camera solves the problem of filming. A charger, an iPad, a patent, all of them solve a problem. My marketing service solved a problem: it got businesses more customers. Solve a problem, make money.

This is the method. Behavioral Demand Psychology. BDP. Every other method out there tells you to just buy this product from China, pick this niche, post these videos, sell this one magic AI automation, and the money appears. Those are business models, and business models run out. Tomorrow, next week, next year. BDP is not a business model. It is a method, and it is built on how money actually works, so it does not expire. And it has a formula.

The formula

Trust × Problem = Money

The more someone trusts you, and the bigger their problem, the more money you make. Picture trust on a scale of 1 to 10. If someone trusts you a 10, they hand you their money and their bank details without blinking. And the size of the problem sets the size of the check.

The two are linked. A bigger problem needs more trust. You do not need to trust someone much to buy a $10 charger. If it breaks, you buy another. But to let someone clean your house, you need real trust, that they will do the job and not steal from you. Bigger problem, bigger check, more trust required. Hold that formula. Everything ahead is built on it.

Two stories about the trust side

Most beginners obsess over the problem side of the equation and treat trust like decoration. So let me show you trust deciding two deals in my own life, one I won and one I lost, because together they will change how you spend your energy.

The $15,000 close from Bangkok

Picture where I was when this deal closed. Bangkok. My MacBook was broken, and money was tight enough that the rent was a genuine question. Not exactly the montage the gurus show you. And from there, in that state, I closed a $15,000 deal.

How? Not charisma. Not a magic script. The client had seen my proof. The case studies, the results, the receipts of work actually done for people like him. On the call, he said it to me almost word for word: "I have seen your proof... so yeah, I should do it." That sentence is the trust side of the equation talking. My circumstances that week were a mess. My evidence was not. And the client was not buying my circumstances. He was buying certainty that his problem would get solved, and the proof carried that certainty for me, all the way from Bangkok, on a broken laptop.

The deal I lost for the same reason

Now the other side, because it taught me more. There was a deal I wanted badly, with a prospect playing at a level I had not documented yet: the $100,000-a-month kind. The conversation was good, the problem was real, my solution genuinely fit. Then he asked the only question that mattered: had I taken someone like him to that level before? I had no testimonial to show at that height. And he looked at me and said: "I don't believe you can help me."

Not "it is too expensive." Not "bad timing." He did not believe. I had no proof at his altitude, no case study showing I had helped someone like him get where he wanted to go. And no sentence I could say in that moment could substitute for the evidence I did not have. The problem was real, remember the formula, but trust was sitting near zero, and anything multiplied by zero is zero. I watched the deal walk out the door.

Here is the ending though. Today I have three case studies of exactly the kind that prospect asked for. And deals like his do not walk anymore. That is the lesson I want burned in: proof is stored trust. Every result you create and document is money sitting in a vault, waiting for a future conversation. Which is exactly why, in Chapter 6, I will make you collect proof from your very first free client. Not for your ego. For the vault.

Trust can be borrowed

One more trust mechanic, and it is the beginner's best friend: trust transfers. You do not have to build every point of trust from zero, because trust flows through people who vouch.

You will meet two of my clients in a moment, twins from the UK. Do you think they messaged a total stranger and handed over their money? No. They had watched my content for months, and I had met one of them in person through a mutual friend. By the time they wrote to me, the trust was already built, quietly, over a long time. That is how most first deals actually happen: through a person or a history, not a cold pitch. Remember it when we get to marketing, because "who do you know that..." is this exact mechanic, weaponized. As a beginner you are trust-poor and connection-rich. Borrow trust before you have earned it.

The four steps of BDP

Now you apply the formula. BDP has four steps, and each gets its own chapter.

Step one, find a problem. Step two, solve and package it. Step three, make them aware. Step four, fulfill. This chapter is step one, finding the problem, plus a look ahead at step two.

Demand and supply, the real meaning

You have heard of supply and demand. Most people misunderstand it, so let me fix that.

To make money you solve a problem, so a problem has to exist. But a problem existing is not enough. Me itching my arm is a problem. I would never pay someone to scratch it. Demand means a problem that people are actually willing to pay to solve. Supply is the other side: is that demand already being met?

Imagine 1,000 people who all want a haircut, and one barber who can cut 10 a day. That leaves 990 people unserved. That is a market with far more demand than supply, and that is exactly what you want. Now flip it: same 1,000 people, but 15 barbers each cutting 50 a day. The demand is almost met, only 250 left. Poor market.

One more layer. Even when supply exists, it might be bad. If those barbers give terrible haircuts and nobody is happy, there is still an opening, to come in and do it better. So you want a market where demand is bigger than supply, or where the supply that exists is not satisfying people. And you serve that market with a service.

Why a service, not a product

Why a service? Because you can start for $0. You do not have to invent and manufacture a product like an iPad, rent a warehouse, or gamble savings on inventory. A service is your skill and your time, and you already own both.

Maybe you are thinking, rich people do not sell their time. True in the way you mean it, but look closer: everyone sells their time, even Elon Musk. He just makes far more per hour he is awake. If you made $1 million an hour, would you sell your time? Of course. It is not about never selling your time. It is about making enough per hour that it is worth it. And even with a product, you are selling the time it took to create it. So you are always selling your time. Sell it wisely.

And there are three more reasons a service is the right first business, and I want you to actually weigh them instead of rushing past. First, you learn fastest by doing the work. A service throws you into real problems, real clients, and real feedback in week one. That education compounds into everything you ever build after. Second, it scales further than people think. You start alone, then AI does the heavy lifting, then systems and people take over the delivery, which is exactly the arc you will see in Chapter 8. Third, done online, it buys all three freedoms at once: financially free, time free, and location free. A barber solves real problems all day and is still chained to one chair in one shop. Your service travels in a laptop. Same formula, different life.

How to find your problem

So how do you find a problem worth solving, one with that lopsided demand? Two ways. Yourself, or Manus. Start with yourself.

Way one: ask yourself. The full Tom and Louis story.

Let me show you way one working on real people, start to finish, because this is exactly how it goes when someone has "no idea what to sell."

Tom and Louis are twins from the UK. Louis was an electrician. They had followed me on Instagram for a long time before they ever messaged me, watching my content, and I had actually met Tom in person, because he used to work with a friend of mine. So by the time they reached out, they already knew who I was. They sent the message every beginner sends: "I want to make money online. What do I do? How do I start? What do I sell?" They did not know where to begin, which is completely normal. So I explained the framework you just learned: we find a problem with lopsided demand, and that is our opening to make money. They liked it. Now came the real work: which problem?

I did not brainstorm business ideas with them. I interviewed them. Here are the actual questions I asked, and this is your list to steal, so answer them yourself as you read:

  • What do you do for work right now?
  • How long have you been doing it?
  • What else have you done? Any other jobs, any businesses you tried?
  • What do you like? What do you hate?
  • What are you good at?
  • When people come to you for help, what do they ask you for?

Nothing clever, just getting to know them. And inside those ordinary answers, the problem was sitting there waiting. Louis, because he had been an electrician for years, had noticed a new UK law: starting April 2026, any tradesperson earning more than 50,000 pounds a year has to report their taxes four times a year instead of once. Read that as a demand machine: hundreds of thousands of UK tradespeople, suddenly facing four times the tax admin, forced to either pay their accountants a lot more or find an easier way. Louis had not read this in a market report. He felt it in his own work. That is what "ask yourself" finds: the problems you have already paid the entry fee to see.

Then the part most people skip. We did not celebrate the idea. We verified it, in three layers. Layer one: Louis himself was living the complaint, one real data point. Layer two: we went hunting in public, Reddit, forums, Facebook groups, to see strangers complaining about the same law in their own words. They were. Layer three: we asked Manus, a research tool (free to use up to a limit, and I am not affiliated), to measure it: how big is this problem, how much demand is there, are people complaining, and are they willing to pay to solve it? Manus confirmed the demand was real.

Then we checked supply. Could the demand already be met? Accountants could handle it, for a lot more money. A few software tools existed, and they were mediocre, with loads of complaints. Demand bigger than the good supply. And note the key point, because beginners get this backwards: someone already solving the problem is a good sign, not a bad one. It is proof of concept. People already pay for this, so you are not guessing, and the bad reviews are your map of what to do better.

So Tom and Louis built the solution: a simple tax-receipt tool. Snap a photo of a receipt on the go, send it to WhatsApp, and it auto-captures everything. They built it with AI in about a week, because building with AI is genuinely easy now, that is pillar two territory and it is coming in the next chapter. And as I write this, the tool is live and moving: 32 signups, their first active user onboard, and more deals booked onto the calendar. Look at what actually happened here: two beginners with zero "business ideas" found real demand by answering ordinary questions about their own life, verified it in public, checked the supply, shipped inside two weeks, and now have a real user base growing. No genius required. A method, run in order.

Way two: ask Manus. The whole flow is four moves.

If you cannot spot a problem in your own life, that is fine. The research tool does the digging, and I already trained it for you. The flow is short enough to memorize:

Run it. Open the Find A Problem prompt from this chapter's resources, fill in your background, and run it in Manus. It does live market research and comes back with 3 to 5 problems where the demand is lopsided and you have an unfair angle. Tell it to take its time.

Read it. Actually read the output, slowly. You are looking for the option that makes you think "wait, I know those people" or "I have felt that." That pull matters, because you will live with this problem daily.

Verify it. Do not trust it blindly. When it names businesses already serving the demand, look them up. Are they good? Good reviews? Professional? What are they not doing? Ten minutes per option. AI research plus your own eyes, never AI research alone.

Write it in one sentence. A verified problem fits this line: "[Avatar] are losing [money or time] because of [specific problem], and the current fixes are [why they fail]." If you cannot fill that sentence, you do not have a problem yet, you have a vibe. Get 2 or 3 sentences like that, and this chapter is done.

The door that is always open: acquisition

If you want to skip all of that, here is one problem that is always in demand and never fully met. Acquisition. Every business, forever, wants more customers and more money. If you help business owners get customers, generate leads, book appointments, raise their sales conversions, you will always be able to make money, because they will always have this problem. If I had to pick one problem for you, this is it.

Summary

  • BDP is a method, not a business model, so it does not expire. It is built on how money is actually made.
  • Someone trusted me with their money to solve their problem: that is where every dollar comes from. Trust times problem equals money.
  • Bigger problem, bigger check, more trust required. The $15,000 Bangkok close and the deal that walked both turned on the same variable: proof. Proof is stored trust, so start filling the vault now.
  • Trust transfers. Tom and Louis reached me through my brother. As a beginner you are trust-poor and connection-rich, so borrow trust through people who vouch.
  • Demand is a problem people will pay to solve. You want demand bigger than supply, or supply that is not satisfying people. Someone already charging for a mediocre version is proof of concept, a good sign.
  • Start with a service: free to start, fastest way to learn, it scales with AI and systems, and online it buys all three freedoms at once.
  • Find the problem by asking yourself (steal the Tom and Louis question list) or by running the trained Manus prompt: run it, read it, verify it, write it in one sentence.
  • If in doubt, pick acquisition. Every business always wants more customers.
Chapter Four
Your Action Steps
1
Fill in the prompt with your background and run it. It surfaces problems where you have an unfair advantage.
2
Pick 2 to 3 problems from the output. Not one, not more than three. Verify each with your own eyes, then post them in the community for feedback.
3
Talk to 10 people who have that problem this week.
Your resource for this chapter
Find A Problem
A trained research prompt that does live market research, verifies demand with real sources, checks the supply, and hands you 3 to 5 problems you are unfairly built to solve. Find it in the community resources for this lesson. Run it, then verify what it gives you.
