title: 5. The Hat Trick Offer
html:
Chapter Five
The Hat Trick Offer
An offer so good your market feels stupid saying no. That is a Hat Trick Offer, and AI can build yours in an afternoon.

Before we build your offer, I have to show you something, because it is the reason gurus fail you and BDP does not.

Remember demand and supply. Say I find out gyms struggle with retention. So I make a YouTube video, "here is how to solve retention for gyms," and a million people watch it. What did I just do to the demand? I flooded it. A million people now chase that same demand, and the opportunity is gone. Wrecked for everyone who watched.

That is why business models keep dying. Even when a guru's method is genuinely the best way today, the moment a million people copy the same 3 steps, the supply and demand is destroyed. Gurus know this. They know it lasts a few months before it is saturated and you are saying the exact same thing to the same avatar as 50 other people.

So how do you win without wrecking it? You bring something of your own. A small change. Go to a sub-niche, martial arts gyms instead of all gyms. Or solve a different problem they have. Just do not copy and paste the viral video, because the opportunity there is already gone.

Why would anyone pick you?

This is the fundamental question of your whole business. You cannot walk up to someone and say "pay me." They will ask, why? How are you different from the last person who said that? If you use the same script, sound the same, and do the same thing, there is no reason to choose you. So they do not. That is why people struggle, and jump from model to model, blaming the niche.

The fix is not a better script. The fix is an offer so good it answers "why you" all by itself.

"Wait, what exactly is an offer?"

Let us define the word before we build one, because most beginners use "offer" to mean "my price," and that mistake alone keeps them broke.

Offer · the complete deal you put in front of someone: the result they get, how they get it, how fast, what they have to do, what it costs, and what happens if it does not work. All of it, in one package.

Your offer is not your service. It is the deal. Two people can sell the exact same service, and one has a deal people fight to accept while the other gets ignored. Same work. Different offer. Different life.

Why do you need one? Because your offer is the only part of your business the market actually experiences before paying you. They do not see your effort, your intentions, or your potential. They see the deal. If the deal is weak, nothing behind it gets a chance.

And when do you use it? Two places, and this is the one-liner to remember: your marketing says the offer, and your pitch explains the offer. That is the whole game. Everything you post, send, and say in the next 2 chapters is just your offer wearing different clothes. Which is why we build it before we build anything else.

A good offer vs a bad offer

Here is the same gym service, packaged twice. Read both like a gym owner who gets 5 messages like this a week.

The bad offer

"I do social media marketing for gyms. I can run your ads and manage your content. My packages start at $500 a month. Let me know if you are interested in working together."

What the gym owner hears: another kid selling activity. What do I actually get? When? What if it fails? He is vague because he is not sure himself. Pass.

 The good offer

"I will put 30 qualified member consultations on your calendar in the next 30 days. You do not write ads, build pages, or chase leads. I handle all of it. If the 30 do not show up, you pay nothing."

What the gym owner hears: a result, a deadline, zero work for me, zero risk. Even if I doubt him, what exactly do I lose? Tell me more.

Look at what changed. Not the service. The service is identical. What changed is that the good offer answers, in 3 sentences, the 4 questions every buyer silently asks: what do I get, how fast, what do I have to do, and what happens if it fails. A bad offer describes you. A good offer describes their new life and removes every reason to say no.

You are probably thinking: sure, but promising "30 in 30 days, or free" sounds terrifying. Good. Hold that fear. In a few pages I will show you the guarantee menu, and the math that makes the fear look silly. First, you need the machine that good offers are built on.

The machine underneath every great offer

For this, I am standing on someone's shoulders, and I will say his name every time. There is a book called $100M Offers by Alex Hormozi. I am not sponsored by him. It is simply the best book ever written on this, the framework here is his, not mine, and when you can afford it, buy the book. What I am giving you is the 80/20 of it, applied for a beginner using AI.

Say the problems you picked last chapter are lead generation for gyms and for roofers. Now you need a solution. As a beginner you do not even know what a good solution contains. That is fine, because AI does. But first, the idea underneath all of it: value.

Value is the dream outcome, times how likely they believe you can deliver it, divided by the time it takes and the effort they have to put in. Four variables. Two you push up. Two you push down. Let me unpack each one, because your entire pricing power lives inside these four words.

Variable 1: Dream outcome (push it up)

The dream outcome is not your service. It is what your service makes possible in their life. A gym owner's dream is not "ads." It is a full gym, a fatter bank account, and the feeling of finally winning. So speak in their dream, not your deliverables. "30 member consultations on your calendar" beats "social media management" every time, because one is a dream with a number on it and the other is a chore with your name on it.

One warning: you raise the dream by being specific, never by inflating. Promise what the math supports. The moment you promise what you cannot deliver, you have left BDP and joined the gurus.

Variable 2: Perceived likelihood (push it up)

This is their belief, on a 1 to 10 scale, that YOU can actually pull it off. Notice the word perceived. It does not matter how good you really are if they do not believe it. This is Trust from Chapter 4 showing up again, in equation form. You raise it with proof, with a guarantee, with a demo they can see, and with how specific you sound. Vague people sound risky. Specific people sound like they have done it before.

"But I have no results yet, so my likelihood is stuck at zero, right?" Wrong. The guarantee exists exactly for you. It moves the risk from their side of the table to yours, which buys you belief you have not earned yet. Keep reading.

Variable 3: Time (push it down)

How long until they feel the result? Every extra week is a discount you are forced to give. 30 days beats 3 months, and "first consultations booked within 7 days" beats both. And here is a beginner trick that costs nothing: even when the full result takes 30 days, engineer a visible win in week 1. The campaign is live, the first leads answered, the calendar has its first name on it. Speed they can see keeps belief alive while the big result cooks.

Variable 4: Effort (push it down)

What do they have to sacrifice to get the result? Hours, staff, new software, learning, stress. Every unit of their effort makes your offer cheaper, and every unit you take off their plate makes it worth more. That is why done-for-you beats do-it-yourself at 10 times the price. The words "you do nothing, I handle all of it" are, per word, some of the most valuable words you will ever say.

Raise the dream and the likelihood. Shrink the time and the effort. That is the whole machine. Every improvement you will ever make to your offer, forever, is one of those four moves. When in doubt, do not get creative. Ask: which of the four am I moving?

Now watch the machine run on two real offers, because this is where it clicked for me.

Two people pitch the same gym. Same dream outcome, same guarantee: if I do not deliver, you get your money back. So far, identical. But person A says it takes 3 months, and the gym has to shoot videos, take photos, and put in 5 extra hours a week. Person B says 30 days, and the gym does nothing, he handles all of it. Who is more valuable? Obviously B. Same result, less time, almost no effort. B can charge far more. Not because B is smarter. Because B's offer scores better on the same 4 dials.

Let AI build it for you

Before AI, you had to reverse-engineer that equation by hand, guessing at what a strong solution even contains. Now you do not. Here is the process.

Do this in Claude

Go to Claude. Create a project. Give the project the book, $100M Offers (buy the ebook and add it). Then tell it:

"I found this problem, [your problem], within this avatar, [your niche]. I want to provide a service that solves it. Use $100M Offers to solve all of their problems and build me the most valuable solution possible."

It sounds simple, maybe even a little scary. That is just how good AI is now, so why would you not use it? Out comes a valuable solution to the problem you found, built on the book's framework.

Pricing: the one thing AI gets wrong

AI is bad at pricing, so you set the price yourself, and it is simple. Look at what your avatar makes. Google it. Say an average gym makes $100,000 a year, and your solution helps them make an extra $20,000 a year. What do you charge? 10% of the value you create. So $2,000 a year, because you make them $20,000. Start at 10%. As you get proof and confidence, raise it.

It works for intangible things too. A couples therapy service: a divorce might cost each partner $50,000, so you are saving them $100,000 together. You can charge $10,000 and easily justify it. Is $10,000 a lot to save someone $100,000? No, because they keep $90,000. That is how you price. Take 10% of the value you create.

I ran the prompt for you. Watch me grade it.

Talking about AI output is cheap, so let me show you the real thing. I ran the exact process above for the gym lead-generation example: a Claude project loaded with $100M Offers, then the prompt with "lead generation" as the problem and "independent gyms" as the avatar. Below is the kind of output you get back, printed so you can watch me grade it. This is a real example run. Yours will come out different, and that is fine. What I want you to steal is the judgment.

Because here is the trap nobody warns beginners about: AI output always LOOKS finished. Clean formatting, confident tone. Most beginners copy it straight into a message and wonder why nobody replies. The pros read it like an editor. Gold parts stay. Weak parts get cut or fixed. Here is what that looks like, block by block.

From the run · GOOD, keep it

"Core promise: We will book 30 qualified member consultations onto your calendar in the next 30 days. A consultation only counts as qualified if the person lives within 15 minutes of your gym and confirmed a time."

Why this is gold: a number, a deadline, and a definition of "qualified" that protects both sides. Specific promises raise perceived likelihood on their own, because vague people sound like they are guessing. Notice it sells consultations, not "marketing."
From the run · GOOD, keep it

"Done-for-you delivery: we write and run the ads, build the landing page, answer every lead within 5 minutes, qualify them, book them, and send reminders so they show up. Your only job: show up to the consultations and do what you already do best."

Why this is gold: it attacks the effort variable line by line, and it ends by handing the gym owner an identity, "do what you already do best." Effort near zero makes the same result worth multiples more. This paragraph alone is most of the offer's value.
From the run · WEAK, fix it

"Our proprietary AI-driven system leverages cutting-edge optimization to maximize your acquisition funnel performance."

Why this is weak: it says nothing. No gym owner has ever wanted an "acquisition funnel," they want members. Corporate words are camouflage for missing thinking, and buyers smell it. Rewrite in human: "we run the ads and fill your calendar." If a sentence could appear on any agency's website, delete it.
From the run · WEAK, cut it

"Gyms using systems like this typically see a 47% increase in monthly recurring revenue within 60 days."

Why this is dangerous: I never gave it that number. AI invents statistics with a straight face. Quote a made-up stat on a call, get asked "source?", and your trust, the biggest variable you own, dies on the spot. Rule: never use a number you cannot personally back. Your real numbers, however small, beat impressive fake ones.
From the run · GOOD, keep it (with the fix below)

"Guarantee: if the 30 qualified consultations are not booked within 30 days, you pay nothing. Condition: you attend the consultations that are booked."

Why this is gold: risk deleted for them, and the condition ties the promise to the one thing only they control, showing up. That single condition is what protects you from the lazy client. More on the guarantee menu in a minute.
From the run · WEAK, override it

"Suggested investment: $1,997 per month (premium positioning tier)."

Why you override this: the number is not reasoned, it is pattern-matched from the internet, which is exactly why I told you AI is bad at pricing. You price it yourself with the 10% rule and your niche's real math. The "premium positioning tier" label is decoration. Delete.
From the run · GOOD, but trim it

"Bonuses: (1) a no-show recovery text sequence, (2) a 5-star review campaign for your gym, (3) a referral script for new members, (4) a social content calendar, (5) a branding audit."

Why: bonuses 1 to 3 attack real side-problems next to the main promise (no-shows, reputation, more members), so they add value. Bonuses 4 and 5 are filler that dilutes. Keep 3 sharp bonuses. A pile of vague ones makes the whole offer feel like a late-night TV ad.

See what happened? The machine did in 3 minutes what would have taken you 3 weeks, AND it made 3 mistakes that would have cost you deals. That combination is the lesson. AI is the fastest employee you will ever have, and it still needs a boss. The boss is you, holding the Value Equation. Every block above got graded against the same 4 dials: dream, likelihood, time, effort. Now you can grade your own run the same way.

Anatomy of a finished Hat Trick Offer

So you know exactly what "done" looks like, here is a complete offer, filled in, for the gym lead-gen example. Yours will differ, but every part below must exist in yours.

A finished offer, line by line

The promise: "I will fill 30 qualified member consultations into your calendar in the next 30 days."

Done for you: "You do not write ads, build pages, or chase leads. My system does all of it. Your only job is to show up to the consultations."

The proof: your demo, your time-and-money story, or your first result. (Chapter 6 shows you proof without a track record.)

The guarantee: "If the 30 consultations do not show up in 30 days, you pay nothing."

The investment: 10% of the value created.

Read those 5 lines again. Dream outcome, effort removed, likelihood raised, risk deleted, price anchored to value. That is the whole Value Equation wearing clothes. And it scores the hat trick from Chapter 4: it gives them what they want, removes what they hate, and removes the risk.

The guarantee menu

Beginners hear "guarantee" and panic. Relax, there are only 4 kinds, and you only need one:

1. Money back. "Hit the result or every dollar back." Strongest trust builder, use it when you are new and hungry.
2. Work free until. "I keep working for free until you get the result." Costs you time, not cash. Great when you are confident but early.
3. Performance basis. "You only pay per result delivered" (per booked appointment, per closed member). Removes all risk, and forces you to get good fast.
4. Conditional. "Guaranteed, as long as you show up to the consultations." Ties the promise to the things only they control. Add this line to any of the first three so a lazy client cannot sink you.

Pick one. Say it in one sentence. If your guarantee needs a paragraph of small print, it is not a guarantee, it is a trap, and they smell it.

"But will people not abuse the guarantee?"

This is the fear that stops 9 out of 10 beginners, so let us kill it with math instead of feelings.

Let's say you run the money-back guarantee at $600 a month, and it helps you close 10 clients this quarter instead of the 4 you would close without it, because the risk stopped scaring people. That is 10 x $600 = $6,000 a month coming in. Now let's say one client, out of the 10, hits a bad month and takes the refund. You give back $600.

Do the subtraction. Without the guarantee: 4 clients, $2,400 a month. With it: 9 paying clients after the refund, $5,400 a month, plus $600 returned once. The guarantee "cost" you $600 and paid you an extra $3,000 a month. Those are "let's say" numbers, plug in your own, but the shape of the math almost never changes: the extra deals a guarantee closes are worth far more than the rare refund it pays. Do not be emotional about it. Do the math.

And the edge case, because there is always one: if someone shows signs of being a refund hunter before you sign them, do not sign them. The guarantee is a trust machine for honest buyers, not a charity for professional abusers. You are allowed to say no to a client. Write that down.

Bonuses: attack the side-problems

A bonus is a small extra you stack on the main promise. Done right, bonuses can make the deal feel bigger than the price all by themselves. Done wrong, they make you look like a TV infomercial. Three rules keep you on the right side (the thinking comes from $100M Offers, the street version is mine):

Rule 1: a bonus must attack a problem that shows up NEXT TO your main promise. You book 30 consultations? Their next problem is no-shows. So bonus: a no-show recovery sequence. After that: turning members into more members. So bonus: a referral script. Each bonus answers a worry they were about to have.

Rule 2: name it and price it. "No-Show Rescue Sequence, worth $400, included free" beats "plus some extra templates." Unnamed value is invisible value.

Rule 3: three sharp bonuses beat seven soft ones. Every weak bonus dilutes the strong ones and adds a smell of desperation. If you would not sell it alone for real money, it is not a bonus, it is clutter.

Scarcity and urgency, the honest versions only

You have seen the fake versions your whole life. "Only 2 spots left!" from a guy with zero clients. A countdown timer that resets at midnight. That garbage is exactly what this book stands against, and buyers got vaccinated against it years ago. But real scarcity and real urgency exist, and you should say them out loud, because true things that help people decide are not manipulation.

Real scarcity is capacity math. You deliver done-for-you. Delivery takes hours. Hours are finite. Let's say each client takes 8 to 10 hours a week and you have 30 work hours: you genuinely cannot serve more than 3 clients well. So say it: "I take 3 clients at a time, one spot opens next month." Every word true. And truth you can defend on a call is worth 10 fake countdown timers.

Real urgency is their math, not yours. Every month a gym runs without a lead system, the empty slots cost real money. "Starting in March instead of February costs you roughly a month of new members" is urgency built from THEIR numbers. You are not pressuring them. You are pricing their delay. There is a difference, and they can feel it.

Anti-guru rule, non-negotiable: if the scarcity is not true, do not say it. One caught lie costs you the only currency this whole book runs on.

Naming basics: clear beats clever

Last piece. Your offer needs a name, because "my services" is not a thing anyone repeats to a business partner. You do not need branding lessons. You need one line: outcome plus timeframe plus who it is for.

"The 30-Day Gym Fill System." "The 30 Consultations Sprint for Independent Gyms." "The Booked Solid Program." Say what it does, how fast, and for whom. Resist being clever. Clever names need explaining, and anything that needs explaining in marketing is losing. The test: if a gym owner hears the name once and can guess what it does, you named it right.

Package it, and build a demo

Now you have a solution, a price, a guarantee, bonuses, and a name. Package it into the final offer. Tell the same Claude project:

Do this in Claude

"Use the full steps inside $100M Offers to build a no-brainer offer for my avatar."

Then grade the output like I showed you above. Keep the gold, cut the fluff, override the price. I could sit here and lecture on every sub-technique for another hour, but the book covers that, and Claude applies it for you. Go apply it.

One bonus step. Use AI to build a quick demo of your solution, so you have something real to show your market. How to actually build and deliver the full thing is pillar four, fulfillment, later in the book. For now, a demo is enough to start.

Summary

  • When a guru teaches a model to a million people, they flood the demand and kill the opportunity. Bring your own angle: a sub-niche or a different problem.
  • Your offer is not your service. It is the complete deal: result, speed, their effort, the price, and what happens if it fails. Marketing says it, the pitch explains it.
  • A bad offer describes you. A good offer describes their new life and answers the 4 silent questions: what do I get, how fast, what do I do, what if it fails.
  • Value equals dream outcome times likelihood, divided by time times effort (credit: $100M Offers by Alex Hormozi). Every improvement is one of those 4 moves.
  • Build the solution and offer with AI, then grade the output: keep specifics, cut corporate words, delete invented statistics, and always override the price.
  • Price at 10% of the value you create. Guarantee from the 4-item menu, and let the math, not your fear, decide.
  • Three sharp bonuses that attack side-problems. Only true scarcity and urgency. Name the offer so clear a stranger can guess what it does.
Chapter Five
Your Action Steps
1
Run the Offer Builder with your problem from Lesson 4.
2
Grade the output like I graded mine: keep the specific, cut the corporate, delete invented numbers, override the price.
3
Read the offer out loud to one real human, for practice.
4
Price it: value created divided by 10. Write the number down. Do not negotiate with yourself. One thing to keep in mind: you have to be able to say the number out loud without flinching. If you cannot, start lower, get your first sales, then raise it.
Pro tip

a. Always have a guarantee, or work on a performance basis, when starting out.

b. Always offer as much done-for-you as possible.

c. But NEVER start working with someone before getting paid, even a $250 setup fee. Or it will not work.

title: 6. Get Seen
html:
Chapter Six
Get Seen
You have done all the hard work already. Now you just have to make people know you exist.

I want to tell you about the 2 most useless weeks of my business life.

I had my offer. Written, priced, guaranteed, sitting in a document. All I had to do was send it to human beings. And for 2 straight weeks, I sent it to nobody. Zero outreach. Instead I "improved the website." I adjusted the logo. I researched my niche a little more, you know, to be thorough. I reorganized my notes. Every night I closed the laptop feeling busy, and every night my revenue was the same round number: zero.

Nobody was going to knock on my door and ask if I happened to have an offer saved somewhere. But that is exactly how I was acting. And when I finally admitted why, it was not strategy. It was fear wearing a busy costume. Sending the offer meant someone could say no. Polishing the logo meant nobody could.

So let me say the thesis of this chapter plainly, because I needed someone to say it to me: a business nobody knows about is a hobby with expenses. By now you know how I got here, the real problem, how to become Version Two, the BDP method, how to find a problem, and how to build a Hat Trick Offer. Pillar three is making your avatar aware you exist. That is all marketing is. You have done most of the work. Now we make it impossible to hide.

What a Hat Trick Offer really is

The one thing this all runs on is your Hat Trick Offer. I come from football, so here is the name. When someone scores 3 goals in one game, that is a hat trick. They get remembered. Man of the match, they take the ball home, it goes in the history books. Your offer needs to score a hat trick, so it becomes unforgettable and your prospect feels stupid saying no.

So marketing is you reaching your avatar and saying: I can get you your desired outcome without the stuff you hate, and here is proof, and here is my guarantee.

Proof when you are a beginner

The best proof is having done it for others. If you are a complete beginner, you do not have that yet. Do not panic, there are 4 other ways to prove you can help.

One, demonstration. Build a demo with AI. Or deliver the first piece of the service free. Or offer a 7 or 14 day free trial. Selling a website? Do not say "I will build you a website." Build it in a day and say "I already built this for you, want it?" It is more work, but as a beginner you have to win trust.

Two, connections. Trust transfers. If you trust me, and I introduce you to my friend who is a fitness coach, you already trust him a little, just because I vouched. So use the people you know to reach the people you want.

Three, time and money. Tell them what it cost you. "I spent 120 hours planning this, and over $53,000 learning it, and now you get it." Suddenly the value feels higher, because they see you did the work and are not bluffing.

Four, association. Associate with what they like and trust. Use the tool they use. Speak their language. If the owner supports Barcelona, wear a Barcelona shirt on the call. Subtle, but people trust people who are like them.

And if you have little proof, you must include a strong guarantee. Simple: if you do not deliver what you promised, they get their money back. Your first $1,000 will not make you rich. The experience and the future business will. So do not get greedy. A guarantee builds a reputation, and the opposite makes people hate you and kills your business. Give what they want, remove what they hate, remove the risk. That is the hat trick.

The 8 ways to market (and your 4)

Here is something that should relax you: there are only 8 ways to market in the entire world. Not 800. Eight. Every tactic you have ever seen a guru sell is one of these 8 wearing a costume.

Warm outreach, cold outreach, content, affiliates, referrals, paid ads, employees, agencies. As a beginner, half are off the table, and knowing WHY protects you from wasting a year. You cannot get referrals with no customers to refer you. You are not hiring employees or agencies with no revenue to pay them. And paid ads are fuel for a machine that already works, not a machine builder, so skip them unless you have $5,000 you genuinely do not care about losing. That leaves your 4: warm outreach, cold outreach, affiliates, and content.

Before we go through your 4, understand why there are only 8 in the first place. It comes down to two simple questions, and this is straight from Hormozi's $100M Leads.

Question one: do these people know you? There are only two kinds of people in the world for your business. People who know you already, friends, family, followers, old customers, anyone who gave you permission to contact them. Those are your warm audience. And people who have never heard of you. Strangers. Those are your cold audience.

Question two: are you talking to one person, or to a room? You can talk privately, one person at a time, like a phone call, a text, or a DM. That is one-to-one. Or you can talk publicly, where many people hear the same thing at once, like a post, a video, or a podcast. That is one-to-many.

Now put the two questions together, and you get four boxes. That is it. That is all the ways any human being can let any other human being know that something exists:

  • One-to-one, to people who know you = warm outreach
  • One-to-many, to people who know you = posting content
  • One-to-one, to strangers = cold outreach
  • One-to-many, to strangers = paid ads

Those four are what you can do yourself. The other four ways, referrals, employees, agencies, and affiliates, are just other people doing those same four things for you. Which is why they come later: you cannot hand someone else a machine you have never run.

One thing that confuses beginners: sending 500 emails with a tool is still one-to-one. A machine is doing it faster, but each email still lands in one person's private inbox. The tool changes the speed. It does not change the type.

So here are your 4, and for each one you get the same 5 things: what it is, why it works for a beginner, when to use it, exactly how to run it, and the resource that does the heavy lifting for you.

Lead · a person who could become your client and who you can actually reach. A name with a door. "Gym owners" is a market. "Marcus from Iron Temple Gym, his Instagram handle, his city" is a lead.

Way 1: Warm outreach. Start here.

What it is: reaching out, one by one, to people who already know you. Friends, family, phone contacts, followers on Instagram and Snapchat, old classmates, any community, email list, or course you have ever been in.

Why it works for a beginner: because trust, the thing that takes longest to build, is already there. Remember the master equation: money flows where trust meets problems. With strangers you start at trust zero. With your network you start halfway up the hill. That is why this is the fastest first money in the game, and why almost every one of my clients makes their first money within 14 to 30 days doing exactly this.

When to use it: first, always, and forever. It is not a beginner phase you graduate out of. Every time you improve your offer or want quick momentum, you run a warm lap.

How to run it: gather everyone you know in one list, or just go app by app. Do not stop at the obvious ones, because the forgotten lists are where the surprises are:

  • Your phone contacts, top to bottom
  • Instagram followers and everyone you follow
  • Your email inbox, sent folder included
  • WhatsApp chats and any group chat you are in
  • Snapchat, Facebook, and LinkedIn if you have them
  • Old school and university class group chats
  • Any Discord, Skool, or Slack community you ever joined
  • Your old teammates, from sports, work, or that job you quit

Then reach out like a normal human. "Hey John, long time no see, heard you finished uni, how are you?" Then, here is the trick most people get wrong. You do not pitch them directly. You ask who they know.

Warm outreach script (fill the blanks)

Hey [name], long time no see. How have you been?

[Have a normal, human exchange first.]

Quick one, [name]. Who do you know that [owns a barber shop / runs a gym / fits your avatar]? I help them [dream outcome] without [the stuff they hate]. Here is my proof: [proof], and I guarantee it, [your guarantee]. Anyone come to mind?

Ask "who do you know that," not "do you know anyone." "Do you know anyone" is a yes or no question, and busy people default to no. "Who do you know" makes their brain search for a name. They say "oh, Andre has a barber shop," and now you have reached your network's network, with trust riding along for free. And if John himself is the avatar, he will often say "wait, that sounds good, how does that work?" So you never have to awkwardly pitch a friend. He asked you.

This one strategy made me multiple six figures. One client, Alfie, made 14,000 pounds in 2 days and 22,000 pounds in 7 days with warm outreach alone. Not because he is magic. Because 15 conversations with half-trust beat 500 messages with zero trust, every time you are new.

Two upgrades before you start. First: if your list is thin or your offer is brand new, offer it free to 1 or 2 people in exchange for a written testimonial and permission to share the results. You are not working for free, you are buying proof, and proof is the exact thing you lack. Second: never end a conversation at zero. Even a "no" can hand you a name. "All good! Who do you know that might want [outcome]?" costs one sentence and keeps the chain alive.

Way 2: Cold outreach. Strangers at volume.

What it is: the same one-to-one game, but with strangers. Calls, emails, texts, and DMs to people who have never heard of you.

Why it works for a beginner: it is the only method where you control the volume completely. No algorithm, no waiting, no budget. You decide to contact 50 humans today, and 50 humans hear about your offer today. It costs time and courage, the 2 currencies every beginner actually has.

When to use it: the day your warm list stops producing conversations, which for most people is week 2 or 3. Warm and cold then run together, every day, as your engine.

How to run it: with strangers you get straight to the point. No "long time no see." An email is simply:

Cold email (fill the blanks)

Hey, I help [avatar] get [dream outcome] without [the stuff they hate], guaranteed. Here is my proof: [proof]. Want to chat?

You need volume, so scrape a list of 1,000 to 5,000 strangers, then call, email, text, or DM. Which is best? By far, ten out of ten times, calling. If you can call your niche, do it. It is the fastest and cheapest, it is free. You can scrape leads with Claude Code plus Apify (search "scrape leads with Claude Code and Apify" on YouTube). If you have $500 to invest, set up an email system with a tool like Instantly to send hundreds of emails a day. Even then, still call the people who reply. And here is the calling framework.

Cold call framework

If a gatekeeper answers: "Hi, is it okay if you can help me with something? I am trying to reach the owner about [the outcome you provide]. Could you put me through?"

When you reach the owner, pitch your Hat Trick Offer: "I help [avatar] get [dream outcome] without [the stuff they hate]. I guarantee it, [your guarantee], and here is my proof: [proof]. Worth a quick call to see if I can do the same for you?"

DM and text use the same framework as the email: get to the point, lead with the Hat Trick Offer. This is exactly why your offer has to be great. A weak offer books no calls. If you are booking calls, your offer is good. The full, expanded scripts for every channel are in your Proven Scripts resource for this chapter.

The pipeline: from "I have an offer" to a booked call

Here is the moment most people get stuck. You have the offer written in a document in front of you. And you sit there thinking, okay, how do I actually get a client from this? So let me remove every gap. First principles: the offer must get in front of your avatar. That breaks into 6 steps, and none of them is vague.

Step 1: pick the platform by where your avatar is easiest to reach. Not your favorite platform, theirs. Gym owners live on Instagram, they have to post there, so DMs reach them. Tradespeople answer their phones, so calls reach them. Corporate types read email. Ask one question: where can I get 50 of them in front of me today? That is your platform. Pick one or two, not five.

Step 2: learn the platform's limits, then do the math. Every platform flags accounts that act like spam bots. On Instagram, as I write this, a normal account can send roughly 25 to 30 cold DMs a day before you risk getting flagged. (These numbers change, the principle never does: find today's limit, stay under it.) So the math is simple: one account is about 25 safe DMs a day, two legit accounts is 50. Warmed, real accounts with posts and a face, not empty burners, because your avatar checks who is messaging them.

Step 3: build your lead list, 100 a day. You already know the tool: Claude Code plus Apify. Tell Claude Code to scrape 100 Instagram gym-owner accounts (or your avatar) per day, with username, name, city, and follower count. There are dozens of 15-minute YouTube tutorials on this exact setup, search "scrape leads Claude Code Apify." No money for tools? Manual works: hashtags, location tags, and competitor followers, 30 minutes a day of copying handles. Slower, still works.

Step 4: track everyone in one sheet. The moment you message more than 10 people, your memory is done. One Google Sheet, one row per lead: name, handle, date of first message, last follow-up date, status (no reply / replied / call booked / closed), and notes. That sheet is your CRM until real money shows up, and it is the difference between "I DM'd some people" and running a machine. I have a ready-made one built exactly for this, the Free CRM in this chapter's resources, so you do not even have to build the sheet.

CRM · stands for customer relationship management. Forget the software aisle: it just means the one place where you track every lead, every conversation, and what happens next. A Google Sheet is a CRM. The point is that nothing gets forgotten.

Step 5: send, then follow up on a rhythm. Send the day's messages using the script from this chapter. Then the part everyone skips: the follow-up is where the money is. Most replies come from message two, three, or four, not message one, because busy owners see a DM, mean to answer, and forget. Follow up the next day, then day 3, then day 7. Short and human: "Hey [name], any thoughts on this?" Log every touch in the sheet. If after four touches nothing, mark them cold and move on, no hard feelings, volume solves it.

Step 6: they replied. Now book the call, fast. The goal of the chat is not to sell in the DMs. It is one line: "This is easier to show than type. Open to a quick 15-minute call this week? I have [day] at [time] or [day] at [time], what works?" Two options, not "when are you free," because two options gets a decision. The moment they pick, you book it, and Chapter 7 takes over from there, including exactly how to set up the calendar invite and make sure they show up.

Now let me show you the math, so you know what to expect and do not panic on day two. Follow it one line at a time:

  • Today you send 50 DMs.
  • Most people ignore you. That is normal. Say 5 of those 50 people write back over the next week, once your follow-ups land.
  • Of those 5 who replied, say 2 of them agree to get on an intro call with you. The other 3 were curious but not ready.
  • So one day of sending 50 DMs gives you roughly 2 intro calls booked.
  • Do that every working day for a month, about 20 days, and you have booked around 40 intro calls.

Those are made-up numbers to show you the shape of the machine. Yours will be different. But look at what they tell you.

On day one you send 50 messages and hear nothing back, so it feels like it is not working. By the end of the month you have a calendar full of calls, built entirely from days that felt like nothing was happening. The machine pays by the month, not by the day. That is why the daily number is not negotiable, and why quitting in week one means quitting right before the payout.

Speed: the cheapest advantage you will ever own

Now let me hand you an edge that costs nothing and beats companies 100 times your size. When a lead replies, you are on the clock, and almost nobody knows how brutally short the clock is.

The Lead Response Management Study, run by Dr. James Oldroyd at MIT, measured what response speed does to a lead. The finding: contact a new lead within 5 minutes instead of 30, and you are 100 times more likely to actually reach them, and 21 times more likely to qualify them. Not percent. Times. A separate Harvard Business Review study of 2,241 companies found the average company takes 42 hours to respond to a new lead, and that companies responding within the first hour were about 7 times more likely to qualify the lead than those that waited longer.

Read those two findings together and you see the gift. The average business, with employees and budgets and software, leaves a hot lead sitting for nearly 2 days. You, a beginner with a phone in your pocket, can answer in 90 seconds. When someone replies to your DM, that notification is not a task for later. It is a fire. Their interest peaks the moment they hit send and decays by the minute. Answer while you still exist in their head, and you beat every slow competitor without spending a cent.

The rule: during your work hours, replies get answered inside 5 minutes. Turn the notifications on. This one habit will win you deals your competitors never even knew they lost.

The Lag Law

Here is the flip side of speed, and if you skip this section, you will quit right before your money arrives. I have watched it happen more times than I can count.

You reply to leads in minutes. But the pipeline as a whole pays slowly, because businesses decide slowly. Owners are busy, they miss messages, they think about it, they talk to a partner, they push the call a week. So the work you do today does not pay today. It pays in 2 to 6 weeks. I call this The Lag Law: today's inputs pay in 2 to 6 weeks, so today's empty bank account is judging work you did a month ago, not the work you did today.

Walk the real timeline of a single lead. Day 1: you send the message. Day 3: they reply, from your day-1 batch, after your follow-up. Day 5: intro call booked and held. Day 7: demo call with the decision makers. Week 2: they push it, someone was traveling, you follow up. Week 3 or 4: yes, invoice, money. Multiply by a whole pipeline and the picture is exact: weeks 1 and 2 of daily outreach feel like shouting into a canyon. Nothing comes back. Then week 3 the first echoes land, and week 5 you are suddenly juggling calls, all from work you did back when it felt pointless.

The Lag Law has 2 commands. First: never judge a day's work by that day's revenue, judge it by inputs sent, because the revenue belongs to a future week. Second, and this is the one that saves you: never stop sending on a good week. The classic beginner death spiral is landing 2 clients, stopping outreach to deliver, and waking up 6 weeks later to an empty calendar, then calling it "the ups and downs of business." It is not. It is the lag punishing a gap you created a month and a half earlier. The machine runs daily or it does not run.

Way 3: Affiliates. Borrow someone's audience.

What it is: a partner who already has access to your market sends you customers, for a cut. Sure, maybe it is not the sexiest or newest system a guru might market online to claim they have found the newest best way to get customers. But it works, and it has always worked.

Why it works for a beginner: it is trust transfer at scale. Chapter 4 taught you that trust can be borrowed. An affiliate is exactly that: their years of relationship with your avatar, rented for a commission. One good partner can outproduce a month of cold DMs.

When to use it: after your offer is proven on at least a client or two, because partners lend their reputation and want to see it is safe. Then it compounds quietly forever.

How to run it: here is the classic example, with the numbers.

A gym owner goes to barbers and says "give your customers this card, they get 15% off my membership, and I will pay you $50 for every one who joins." The member gets a deal, the barber gets $50, and the gym gets a member worth $700 for about $100 in cost. Seven times the money. Ten of those a month is $6,000 in profit from one partnership.

To get affiliates, list everyone with access to your market, barbers, accountants, lawyers, agencies, then warm or cold outreach them, exactly like you learned above. But you must make it easy: bring the cards, the system, the training. And give the affiliate their own Hat Trick Offer, because they will not do extra work for nothing. Give them what they want, remove the hassle, guarantee it. Partner acquired.

Way 4: Content. One to many.

What it is: one video, seen by a thousand people. You talk once, the platform repeats you forever.

Why it works for a beginner: content is outreach that compounds. A DM dies when it is read. A video keeps selling you next month. It also warms up every other method: prospects check your profile before replying, and a profile with real content raises your perceived likelihood before you say a word.

When to use it: start now, expect nothing for weeks. Content obeys the Lag Law harder than anything else in this chapter. It is a snowball, not a light switch.

How to run it: pick one platform, post one a day. Three questions decide everything: what do I post, how do I write it, how do I record it.

Ideas come from four places:

  • Your own life. What you did today, what you figured out, what went wrong.
  • What you are learning. Books, courses, this one included. Teach it the day you learn it.
  • What your avatar is already talking about. Forums, Facebook groups, YouTube comments, reviews. Their words, handed to you.
  • A Claude Code agent. Set it up once to scrape Reddit, Twitter, and YouTube comments from your avatar, and it hands you fresh ideas whenever you ask. This is the best of the four.

Structure is always the same three parts:

Part 1 · The hook
The first line. This is everything. If the hook is weak, nobody sees part 2, no matter how good it is.
↓
Part 2 · The body
You deliver exactly what the hook promised. Not something near it. The thing itself.
↓
Part 3 · The end
Either a simple call to action ("comment the word tool and I will send it"), or you just stop, because you already delivered.

The one rule you cannot break: never fail to deliver what the hook promised. Do it once and they will not watch you again.

Long-form video is the same thing on repeat: hook, body, hook, body, hook, body. Like scenes in a movie.

Hooks: do not invent your own. Find winning ones. Here is the process:

  • Scroll YouTube and Instagram and collect 50 to 100 hooks that are clearly outperforming everything around them. This takes about an hour.
  • Save them all in one document.
  • Give Claude Code your idea plus that list, and tell it to match your idea to the 8 to 10 best hooks. Match, not write.
  • Pick your favorite and use it.

To skip the collecting entirely, The Hook Bank in this chapter's resources is my own running collection, already sorted.

Recording needs almost nothing:

  • Your phone. That is the camera.
  • A cheap tripod, or lean it against something.
  • Light from a window, or a ring light if it is dark.
  • Front-facing camera. Talk to it like you are talking to one person.
  • Cut the dead air, add captions, post.

That is the whole setup. Post a lot and you will get good fast. Nobody has ever gotten good by buying a better microphone.

"But I am scared to post." Good. Let us take that apart.

Every beginner carries the same 3 beliefs about posting, so let me put them on the table where we can look at them. One: "who am I to post? I have no results." Two: "people will laugh at me." Three: "my family and friends will see it and think I am weird." I had all 3. Most of my clients had all 3. Run them through Chapter 3: whose voices are those? Are those people where you want to be? Exactly.

Now the facts. One: you are not posting as a guru, you are documenting what you are building and learning, and documenting requires zero authority. Two: here is what happened when I posted my very first video. It was 11 seconds long. Eleven. It got over 1,000 views, and the laughing mob I had pictured never showed up, because strangers are busy and the algorithm does not care about your nerves. Three: the family question. Some relative may raise an eyebrow for a week. Meanwhile the algorithm shows your video to gym owners in cities you have never visited. You are trading a week of mild awkwardness for a machine that introduces you to your market while you sleep. Bro, take the trade.

Document the climb: Oscar's month

Let me make "documenting" concrete, because it is the single best content strategy for a beginner and almost nobody uses it.

Oscar is one of my students. When he started posting, he had 64 followers. Sixty-four. No results to show, no fancy camera, and every fear you have right now. So he did not pretend to be an expert. He documented the climb. What he was building that day. What he learned. What went wrong. Plain videos of a real person doing the real work.

One month later he had grown past 336 followers, and here is the number that matters: he was booking 1 to 3 calls a day from that tiny audience. Not because 336 is a big number. Because the RIGHT 300 people watching a real person solve real problems trust him more than a million strangers trust a guru. Small and real beats big and fake, and it is the one contest where the beginner starts with an advantage: you have a climb to document, and the guru does not.

So your content plan is not "become an influencer." It is: post the climb, daily, on the platform where your avatar lives. Day 30 you will have proof of work no competitor can fake, an audience that warms every DM you send, and a habit that compounds for years. To remove the last excuse, The First Posts Pack in this chapter's resources gives you your first 10 posts, mapped out: the formats, the angles, and the exact structure for each, built for someone starting from zero.

Summary

  • A business nobody knows about is a hobby with expenses. Marketing is making your avatar aware you exist, and it all rides on your Hat Trick Offer.
  • No proof yet? Use demonstration, connections, time and money spent, and association. Always add a guarantee.
  • There are only 8 ways to market. Beginners run 4: warm outreach, cold outreach, affiliates, and content.
  • Warm first: ask "who do you know that," never "do you know anyone." It reaches your network's network with trust attached.
  • Cold is a 6-step pipeline: platform, limits, list, sheet, send and follow up on day 1/3/7, book with two time options. The follow-up is where the money is.
  • Speed is a free advantage: per the MIT Lead Response Management Study, replying in 5 minutes instead of 30 makes you 21 times more likely to qualify a lead. Answer inside 5 minutes.
  • The Lag Law: today's inputs pay in 2 to 6 weeks. Judge days by inputs, and never stop sending on a good week.
  • Affiliates rent you trust at scale: make it easy and give the partner their own Hat Trick Offer.
  • Content compounds: steal winning hooks, deliver what you hooked, post the climb daily. Documenting beats pretending, and Oscar's month proves a tiny real audience books real calls.
Chapter Six
Your Action Steps
1
List 100 people you know (phone, IG, LinkedIn, email). Yes, 100. It takes 30 minutes.
2
Send the warm script to 100 of them today.
3
Book your daily volume: 100 warm messages OR 100 cold outreaches, every day, calendar-blocked. Answer every reply inside 5 minutes.
4
Use the Google Sheet CRM to track every lead and every follow-up, so the machine never depends on your memory.

title: 7. Sell Like a Doctor
html:
Chapter Seven
Sell Like a Doctor
Sales is not convincing. It is helping the person in front of you make the best decision for them, even if that means not buying. A doctor diagnoses before they prescribe. So do you.

Let me tell you about a sales call I still remember, two or three years later.

I was selling marketing services to gyms. Not my first call, I had done a bunch by then, which is part of why it stung. Forty, forty-five minutes on a call with this guy, and I pitched. That is all I did. I had slides, so I went through them. Next slide, next slide, explaining, presenting, pitching.

Then, before I gave him the price, I asked what I thought was a safe question. "Do you feel like this could actually help you?"

He said no.

I did not see it coming at all. In my head I was going, no, no, no, what do you mean no? I thought that was a good pitch. I did not say that out loud. What I said was, "how come?" And he told me, plainly: it does not make sense to me, it does not fit me. Then we ended the call.

It was a horrible call. And notice that I still remember it years later, because here is what I had done. I spent forty-five minutes talking, and I never found out what he actually needed. So of course my solution did not fit him. I had never asked what he would be fitting it to.

Sales is helping the person in front of you make the best decision possible for them, even if that means not buying your stuff. That is it. It is not manipulation, shouting, harassing, tricking, or lying. You are a problem finder and a problem solver, exactly like BDP taught you. On a call, you are a doctor: you diagnose before you prescribe.

The two-call close

You sell on calls. Your marketing from the last chapter brings you people who are interested and ask "how does this work?" You reply: "How about a quick call/Google Meet and I show you? Would that help?" They say yes, and you book it. And here is the structure that makes everything work: you split the sale into two calls.

Call 1: the intro call · one job: discover everything

Where they are. Where they want to go. What is stopping them. Whether they even have a problem you can solve. You ask, they talk, you take notes.

The one rule: you do not pitch here. Not the price, not the features, not "a quick overview." Nothing. A doctor does not sell surgery during the X-ray.

If the intro call surfaces a real problem you can fix, you end it with the transition line. Word for word:

The transition line (end of call 1)

"[Name], I know exactly how to help with this. It is easier to show than tell, so let us book a short demo call where I walk you through it, built around your situation. I have [day] at [time] or [day] at [time], which works better? And who else should be there so you can make the decision together?"

Call 2: the demo call · one job: show the bridge and pitch

You walk them through your solution, tailored to what call 1 uncovered, in their language, aimed at their numbers. This is where the pitch lives.

The one rule: all decision makers present. Business partner, spouse, whoever shares the money decision. No exceptions.

Why is the decision-makers rule non-negotiable? Because pitching half the decision is how you get "let me talk to my partner," and "let me talk to my partner" is where deals go to die. Not because the partner is against you, but because your pitch cannot survive being retold. The prospect will compress your 10 minutes into one clumsy sentence over dinner, the partner hears the price without the value, and the no arrives by text 2 days later. You already asked who else decides, in the transition line. If the partner cannot make it, move the demo. A moved demo closes. A retold demo does not.

And why two calls at all? Three reasons, all working for you. It positions you as someone who prepares, which raises perceived likelihood before the pitch even starts. It gives you time to tailor the demo to their exact situation instead of performing a generic one. And it filters: people who will not book a second call were never going to buy, and now they cost you 20 minutes instead of a whole pitch. Diagnosing and prescribing in one breath feels like a doctor recommending surgery 2 minutes after you sit down. Nobody trusts that doctor.

The rest of this chapter teaches the intro call, because it is where deals are actually won. The demo call runs on the Demo Call Template in your resources, and every pitch rule below applies to it.

The intro call: the island and the bridge

The whole intro call fits in one picture. They live on an island they do not like. There is an island they want to reach. Your solution, later, is the bridge. But you cannot build a bridge before you have mapped both islands, and the water between them.

So the call has four jobs, in this exact order. Do not skip ahead, and do not rearrange them:

  • Job 1. Find out exactly where they are today.
  • Job 2. Find out exactly where they want to be, and why.
  • Job 3. Find out what has stopped them from getting there already.
  • Job 4. Pitch, on the second call, once you know all three.

Jobs 1 to 3 happen on the intro call, and they are almost entirely questions. Job 4 happens on the demo call. Here is each one, with the exact words.

Job 1. Where are they now?

Understand where they are. Ask real questions and listen.

Current situation questions

Can you tell me a bit about your business right now? [listen]

What made you jump on this call today? What is going on, what is the problem? [listen]

How long has it been like this? [listen]

Where are you at now, in numbers? Revenue, customers a month? [get real figures]

Job 2. Where do they want to be?

Now, where do they want to go, and why.

Desired situation questions

Where do you want to be? What would that look like in numbers? [e.g. $100k, 500 customers]

Why that? Why is it important to you? [the real why]

Why now, and not later? [listen]

Then play it back so they feel understood: "So if I have it right, you are here at $10,000 a month with 50 customers, and you want 500 customers to reach $100,000, so you can spend more time with your family. Correct?" When they say "yes, that is right," you have alignment.

Job 3. What has been stopping them?

This is what separates real closers from people who just pitch and hope. Hope is not a strategy. Before you position your bridge, find out why they have not crossed already, because that reason is the real objection. And notice what you are really doing here: you are pulling the real reason into the open while there is still time to talk about it together. Ask after the pitch instead, and the same reason comes back wearing a costume ("I need to think about it"), and costumes are much harder to talk to. In a few pages I will show you exactly what is hiding under those costumes.

The pre-handle

Why is this problem not solved yet? What has been holding you back from getting there? [they answer, e.g. "I do not have time"]

[Dissolve the surface answer.] I hear you. Would you agree everyone has the same 24 hours? And there are owners at $100k with the same 24 hours, right? So what do you think is the real difference between the ones who broke past $10k and the ones who stayed? [they say: "spending time on the wrong things"]

Right. So it is not really time. So what is actually holding you back from getting help and getting there? [now the real objection surfaces, e.g. "I do not trust people with solutions"]

That is the real objection. Dig into it gently. Then make them feel the cost of staying: "If nothing changes, where are you in 3 to 6 months?" Let them say it. "Is that something you are willing to settle for?" "No." "Why not?" Now they are talking themselves toward change. Then paint the other island: "So once we get past this, what changes for you?" "I would be able to do X and Y." "And why does that matter?" Now they see it.

Job 4. The pitch (on the demo call)

You did jobs 1 to 3 on the intro call. You know where they are, where they want to be, and the real thing that has stopped them. Now the demo call has one job: show them the bridge, and let them decide to walk on it.

Run it in five parts, in order.

Part 1 · Play back what they told you
Open by repeating their situation in their own words. "Last time you said you are at 50 members, you want 200 by next year, and the thing in the way has been X." They confirm. Now they know this was built for them, not pulled off a shelf.
Part 2 · Walk them through the solution, in three parts
Three. Not ten. Say "here is how I would help you: one, two, three," and explain each one aimed at what they told you. Keep the whole thing between 5 and 12 minutes. Past 15 minutes nobody is listening.
Part 3 · Check that they believe it before any number
"Do you feel like what I just walked you through would help you get [their goal] and get rid of [their problem]?" If yes, ask "what makes you say that?" and let them explain it back to you. They are now selling themselves, in their own words, which is worth more than anything you could have said.
Part 4 · Name the investment
Only once they believe it works. Never call it the price. Call it the investment, because they get a return on it.
Part 5 · Go straight to next steps
Do not name a number and then go silent. "Here are the next steps. We handle the investment, then I will need access to [whatever you need], and my team and I get to work." Make the yes easy to act on.

Two rules that decide whether this works.

Rule one: never stack a price on a soft yes. If part 3 comes back even slightly hesitant, a "yeah... I mean, yes" instead of a real one, stop and call it out. "You sound a little unsure, what is on your mind?" Fix the doubt first. If they do not believe you can help them, and then you attach a price to it, all you have done is give them a bigger reason to say no.

Rule two: pile on features and you lose. "We do this, and this, and this, and this, and this" does not sound like more value. It sounds like more to think about, and thinking about it is exactly what you do not want. Every extra item you add is another thing they now have to weigh before deciding. Three parts. Punchy. Done.

The mechanics: booking, reminders, and show-ups

A booked call that does not happen is worth zero, so here is the boring plumbing that beginners skip and pros never do.

Booking it, step by step. Get their email in the chat ("what is the best email for the invite?"). Open Google Calendar, create an event, add their email as a guest, and turn on Google Meet, the link generates itself. Free Google Meet gives you 60 minutes per call, which is plenty. If you have $10 a month, get Google Workspace so your invite comes from you@yourbusiness.com instead of a hotmail, it quietly raises trust. Send the invite the moment they pick a time, while you are still talking, and say "just sent it, can you accept it real quick?" An accepted invite triples the odds they show, because now it is in their calendar, not their memory.

The reminder sequence. People miss calls for all kinds of reasons. What you can control is that the time, the day, and the link are sitting in front of them, so you do not miss a call because someone forgot. So you send four short texts, because texts get read (a normal SMS or iMessage, not another email they will ignore). These are for an AI service, so change the middle line to match what you sell:

Reminder texts (adapt to your service)

On booking: "Hey [name], call confirmed for [day and time]. We will look at one thing that could run smoother for you this week, no tech talk. Here is the link: [link]"

24 hours before: "During tomorrow's chat: we will talk about simple ways to save time without hiring or adding tools."

3 hours before: "See you later. No need to prepare anything."

10 minutes before: "I am on the call now: [link]. Join when ready."

Notice how little they ask of the prospect. No homework, no forms, no "come prepared." Every text lowers the effort of showing up, and the 24-hour one quietly tells them what they get out of it. Send them manually at the start, it takes 30 seconds each, and automate later.

Before you join, check three boxes: they have the link, you both have the same time (time zones kill calls), and the right people are coming. If they no-show: do not sulk, and do not accuse them. Take the blame yourself and move the call. Text this:

The no-show text

"Oh my bad [name], I am running behind today, I was just onboarding a new client. Let us push our call to tomorrow, same time. Let me know if that works for you too."

Look at what that does. Now it looks like you missed it, not them. Nobody has to feel guilty or explain themselves, and the call is already rebooked. You stay in charge of the calendar.

If they still go quiet and miss the new time, call them first thing the next day. If you still hear nothing after that, cancel the slot and let them know it is because you gave it to someone else. Said calmly, that is just the truth, and it is the most attractive thing you can say to someone who has been ignoring you.

Why good people say no to good solutions

You now know how to run the calls. So before we handle objections, you need to know what an objection actually is underneath, because it is almost never what they say it is.

If your solution is genuinely the best thing for them, why would they not just buy it? Chapter 3 already gave you the answer, because your prospect is running the exact same machine you are.

Remember it: experiences build beliefs, beliefs build identity, identity chooses actions. Your prospect has a Version One too, and it defends itself just like yours does. So when a good buyer refuses a good solution, it is almost never the solution. It is one of 2 blockers, and both live in their machine, not in your offer.

Blocker 1: limiting beliefs. "AI is a scam." "It will hack me." "That will not work for my business." Where did those come from? Same place yours did: an initial experience, a story from a friend, a headline, then confirming experiences stacked on top. The belief is not stupid, it is protective. But if they believe AI is a scam, they will not buy your AI service, even though it would save them 10 hours a week. The belief decides before the value gets a vote, exactly like your money beliefs once decided for you.

Blocker 2: fear. The same two you met in Chapter 3, wearing business clothes. Fear of failure: "what if I pay and it does not work, what does that say about me?" And fear of success: "what if it works, and I have to grow, hire, change?" Both freeze the same muscle: the decision.

Now the part that changes how you sell forever. You cannot argue someone out of a belief, and you cannot logic someone out of a fear. You know this from your own war with Version One. Being told "just do not be scared" never moved you one inch. What moves people is being helped to SEE the belief, question where it came from, and look at the evidence together. So your job on a call is not to erase the blockers. It is to surface them, gently, and think through them together, like a doctor walking a nervous patient through a scan. That is why the structure you are about to learn is built entirely out of questions.

Objections are just thinking out loud

Then they either pay or say "let me think about it." Do not stress about objections. An objection is not "I hate you." It is the person thinking out loud, and your job is to help them think. Usually the best decision for them is to solve the problem now, not in two months, and you help them see that. Not by talking over them and listing features, but by understanding them.

Handling any objection

[They say: "I need to think about it," or "maybe August."]

Totally fair. What makes you feel August is better than now? [listen fully]

[See it from their side, then offer your perspective.] Here is how I would look at it... [your perspective]

Often they prefer your perspective, and you move forward. Ignore the flashy objection-handling tricks on Instagram. They do not work. Questions do.

Answer questions with questions

Here is the story that taught me the single most useful sentence-level skill in sales. I was helping run leads for a fitness business, and the same message kept landing in the inbox: "What are the diets like?"

Watch the beginner answer it, because I did this first. The lead asks about diets, and you, eager to be helpful, send the encyclopedia. "We offer keto, vegan, vegetarian, Mediterranean, flexible dieting, and we customize macros based on..." A wall of text. Proud of it, too. And what comes back? Nothing. Or worse: "hmm, I do not really like strict diets." You just handed them something to object to. You answered a question you did not understand, so every extra word was a coin flip. Objection created, out of pure helpfulness.

Now watch the doctor answer the same message. "We have a few variations. What got you asking about the diets?" One line. And the reply comes back: "I am vegan." There it is. The real question was never "list your diets." It was "will this work for someone like me?" Now you know exactly what to say: "Perfect, we have full vegan plans, some of our best results are on them. Want me to show you how it would look for you?" Same lead, same product, completely different conversation, because the question behind the question got answered.

So make it a reflex: when a prospect asks you a question, answer it with a short answer plus a question back. "Do you offer X?" "Yes, a few versions. What makes you ask?" You stay in the doctor's chair, you learn something real every exchange, and you never again write a wall of text that talks a buyer out of buying.

How to actually get good at this

Put sales in your ears daily: podcasts, YouTube, books. But the fastest way to improve is to record and rewatch your own calls. Use Fathom, a free note-taker (search "Fathom note taker"), and put it in every call. You will watch yourself and think "why did I say that," and that is exactly how you fix it. There is no other way to catch it. My first recorded call was painful to watch, which is exactly why watching it worked.

The myths that lose the sale

People think selling means talking a lot. My 97% disaster call is what that belief buys you. Wrong. The prospect talks 70% of the time. You talk 30%. Professionals do not win with arguments, they win with questions. Good questions make the prospect feel heard and understood, and make you look like the expert who is calm and in control.

Look like them and sound like them, no backwards hat unless you are selling to skaters. Do not pitch the second you get on. The only time you talk and pitch is during the pitch itself. The rest of the call, you listen and you ask. That is sales. Listen more than you talk, help them make the best decision, and make it easy for them to take the step.

Summary

  • Sales is helping someone make the best decision for them, even if that means not buying. Diagnose before you prescribe.
  • Good prospects say no because of two blockers: limiting beliefs and fear, the same machine from Chapter 3. Surface them and think through them together. You cannot argue anyone out of a belief.
  • Split the sale in two: the intro call discovers everything and never pitches. The demo call pitches, tailored, with every decision maker present. "Let me talk to my partner" means the pitch got retold, and retold pitches die.
  • Run the intro call as the island and the bridge: current island in numbers, desired island in numbers, then why they have not crossed yet. That answer is the real objection. Pre-handle it before any pitch.
  • Pitch in three parts, 5 to 12 minutes, on the demo call. Call it the investment. Confirm they believe it works before you name it.
  • An objection is the prospect thinking out loud. Help them think with questions. And answer their questions with a short answer plus a question back: the diets story is the proof.
  • Record every call with Fathom and rewatch it. Let the prospect talk 70%, you 30%.
Chapter Seven
Your Action Steps

2

3
After each call, score yourself: did they talk 70%? Did you handle the objection before pitching? Did you answer their questions with questions?
