title: 8. Make Them Stay
html:
Chapter Eight
Make Them Stay
A client decides in the first 48 hours whether they will stay with you for years. Win those 48 hours.

You found the problem, built the solution, picked your niche, ran your outreach, and closed your first deal. Now you have a client you have never delivered for. It feels overwhelming. So we go step by step, and the first step matters more than any other.

Onboarding: the first 48 hours

Onboarding is the most important step, because within the first 24 to 48 hours a client quietly decides whether they like you and whether they want to keep working with you. And you want them to stay for a long time.

Understand what is happening on their side of the screen, because it explains everything in this chapter. The moment someone pays you, a silent countdown starts in their head. They just handed money to a person they barely know, and their brain immediately begins hunting for evidence, in both directions. Every fast reply, every visible piece of progress: "good, I chose right." Every hour of silence: "did I just get scammed?" Buyers call it buyer's remorse. I call it the silent countdown, and here is the rule it gives you: in the first 48 hours, silence is not neutral. Silence is evidence against you. You do not need to have delivered anything yet. You need to be visibly in motion.

So make onboarding great. Two rules. First, make it personalized, a one-on-one call, not a cold automated form. Second, make them do as little as possible, as fast as possible. Do not send a giant questionnaire because it "looks professional." Do not ask for their website, find it yourself. If there are things you genuinely need, their card, an invite, access to a platform, do it with them on the call. Share screens and guide them through it. If it is your first time, prepare: watch the YouTube video on how to get access to that software, keep notes beside you, and walk them through calmly.

The first 48 hours, written out

Here is the sequence, hour by hour, so there is nothing to figure out. Run it on every client, even the free ones, because free clients turn into testimonials and referrals only if the experience is paid-level.

Hour 0, the moment they pay: send a short personal message within minutes, not a template blast. "Welcome in, [name]. Genuinely excited to work on [their goal]. Booking your onboarding call now, here are two times." Speed here is the first proof they made the right call.

Hours 0 to 24, the onboarding call: one on one, screens shared. You already know the rules: they do as little as possible, you do everything with them live (accesses, accounts, payments), and you come prepared with your notes on the exact clicks. End the call by telling them precisely what happens next and when: "By [day], you will have [first deliverable]. I will update you before then either way."

Hours 24 to 48, the first win: ship something visible inside two days. Not the whole project, a piece they can see: the ad drafts, the first version of the tool, the list built, the system connected. Send it with a one-line note: "First piece done, ahead of schedule. Next up: [next step]." A client who sees motion in the first 48 hours relaxes for months. A client who hears silence for a week starts drafting the refund email in their head.

Then, forever: the weekly update. Every week, same day, three lines, sent without being asked: what got done, what is next, and anything I need from you. Ninety percent of "my agency ghosted me" horror stories are actually "nobody told me what was happening." Three lines a week makes you the most communicative provider they have ever hired, and it costs you two minutes.

Your first client ever: the honest walkthrough

Because the first one is scary, here is exactly what it looks like. You closed a gym on the lead-gen offer. The moment of panic arrives: "I have never done this before." Good. Here is the order of operations:

Step 1 · Run the onboarding call
The call from the section above. Get every access you need in one sitting, with them on screen share. Do not leave that call needing to email them for logins.
Step 2 · Study the good competitors
Someone already delivers this service well. Find them, and read their reviews. The reviews tell you exactly what clients love and what makes them leave.
Step 3 · Plan it with Claude Code before you build
Open Claude Code and describe, in plain words, what you need to build. Let it plan the delivery with you first. Planning takes ten minutes and saves you two days.
Step 4 · Ship something visible in 48 hours
Not the whole project. One piece they can see, plus the one-line note telling them what is next.
Step 5 · Work the plan and stay ahead
Send the weekly three-liner every week, and solve the next problem before the client notices it exists.

That is the whole job. You will be slow the first time, and that is fine. Slow with communication beats fast with silence. By client three, the panic is gone.

The lesson that made me $28,000: work they cannot see does not exist

Let me tell you about the week I almost lost a client while doing excellent work for him.

Early on, I had a client whose campaigns I was managing well. Genuinely well. I was in his account almost daily, checking the ads, protecting the winners, testing angles. But I did all of it silently, and my weekly report went out late. In my head, the work spoke for itself. Then a message landed: he wanted to talk. On the call I could hear it in his voice, the doubt, the "what am I even paying for." My work had been invisible, so as far as he could tell, it did not exist. The report being late did not read as "busy." It read as "nothing to report."

That week rewired me. The fix was almost embarrassingly small: I started narrating the work I was already doing. A WhatsApp group with each client, and short messages as I worked. "Checked your ads today, the winners stay untouched." "Got an idea for your offer, testing it this week." "Report coming Sunday." Ten seconds to type. And every Sunday, without fail, the weekly report went out, same day, same format, before anyone asked.

The result of those ten-second messages? That client stayed with me for 3 years and paid me over $28,000 in total. One client. Not because the work got better, the work was always good. Because he could finally SEE it. Small updates, massive trust. Your client cannot read your effort. They can only read your messages. So narrate the work. It is the cheapest retention system ever invented.

Same month, two agencies

To make it unmistakable, here is the exact same month of work, delivered by two providers. Same tasks completed, same results produced. Read it as the client.

The silent provider's month

Week 1: nothing. Week 2: nothing. The client messages "how is it going?" and gets "all good, working on it" a day later. Week 3: nothing. Week 4: the invoice arrives, on time, somehow the only thing that is.

What the client is thinking: "Are they even doing anything? I am paying for a black box. Maybe I should ask that other agency what they would charge."

 The narrating provider's month

Day 2: first visible piece ships. Every few days, a ten-second WhatsApp note about what just got done. Every Sunday: the three-line report, done, next, needed. Week 4: the invoice arrives after 8 small proofs of work.

What the client is thinking: "They never stop working. Honestly, for everything they do, this feels cheap."

Same work. Different communication. Different outcome. One of these providers gets churned at the first rough month, the other gets 3 years and $28,000. Decide now which one you are, because the choice is made in your habits, not in your skills.

Deliver with AI

Now you deliver. The service is different for everyone, lead generation, tracking automation, a booking system, whatever you sell. But we lean on AI, and the tool is Claude Code. Talk to it in plain text, and it does the work in code. You do not need to know how to code. I still cannot really code, and I have automated almost my entire business with it. My marketing and sales run themselves, so most of my day is just taking care of clients.

How do you know what a good service even looks like? Look at your competitors. Someone has already solved this problem for your avatar. Study how they did it and steal the good ideas. Just study the good ones with good reviews, not the ones people complain about.

Become the obsessed one

Then you have to actually get good at it. There is no way around this. When I sold marketing to gyms, I became obsessed. I listened to Alex Hormozi's Gym Launch Secrets podcast over and over, in the car, on walks, while training. I bought two books about gyms. I watched endless YouTube on gym acquisition, gym retention, all of it. I am not a gym owner, and I would bet I knew more about running a gym than most gym owners, because I got obsessed with serving my clients. That is the job. It is a daily, ongoing process, and you cannot run from it.

Delivering a good service is the most important part of the whole business. If your service is bad, what are you even going to pitch? "Pay me for my bad work"? Make sure you are not selling garbage.

Overdeliver by being proactive

Do not just deliver. Overdeliver. And the way you overdeliver is by being proactive instead of reactive.

When a client is unhappy, the weak move is to blame: the client did not do their part, the market, the platform, the algorithm. What do you get from that? Nothing. The strong move is to take ownership, even when it was partly the client's fault. Ask yourself, "what could I have done to prevent this?" Maybe you just needed to communicate more. Now you learn, and you keep the next client.

And solve the next problem before it arrives. Say you are building an AI appointment setter for a client. You know the next step is connecting it to their CRM. Do not wait for them to ask "how do we connect this." While you are still building, ask for their CRM access, so it is ready the moment you need it. You planned the solution, so you already know every next step. Always stay one step ahead of your client. They have the problem, you have the solution, so act like it. Keep learning about your client's world, every week, forever.

What overdelivering looks like in real life

Two examples from my own delivery, so this is not theory.

One client needed better ad creatives, and the real fix was fresh footage. I could have sent an email explaining what to film and waited 3 weeks for shaky vertical clips. Instead I drove there and filmed the ads with him, free, no line on the invoice. Another client had a quiet reputation problem: great gym, thin reviews. Nobody asked me to fix it. I built and ran a review campaign as a surprise bonus, because more 5-star reviews made my ads convert better anyway, so his win was my win.

Do the math on gestures like these. A day of filming cost me maybe 6 hours. It bought a client who felt, correctly, that I cared more about his gym than anyone he had ever paid, and clients who feel that do not shop around, do not nickel-and-dime you, and tell their friends. Cheapest marketing I ever did.

One honest caveat so you do not misuse this: these unscalable moves are a beginner's superpower, and a scaling business's trap. With 1 to 5 clients, drive there, film the ads, run the surprise campaign, be unreasonably present. That is exactly the stage you are in, so exploit it. Later, with 15 clients, you cannot drive anywhere weekly, so the care gets built into systems instead: the WhatsApp habit, the Sunday report, the surprise bonus becoming a standard part of month one. Same care, different container. But do not skip the unscalable stage. It is where your reputation gets built.

Your tech stack

Keep it simple. Claude Code to build and automate. GoHighLevel for everything operational: it has your CRM, automations, calendar, forms, and funnels in one place, so you do not need Calendly or a separate email tool. Google Workspace for Sheets, Docs, Meet, and Calendar. For payments, I use a few because my clients are worldwide, but if I pick one for you, start with Commas: easiest to set up and low fees. If you run a community, Skool can even be your payment method, with lower fees still. That is the whole stack. Now go deliver.

Summary

  • Onboarding is the most important step. The silent countdown starts the moment they pay, and in the first 48 hours silence is evidence against you.
  • Make onboarding personal and one-on-one, make the client do as little as possible, and ship a visible first win inside 48 hours.
  • Work they cannot see does not exist. Narrate the work: the WhatsApp habit plus the Sunday report turned one client into 3 years and $28,000.
  • Deliver with Claude Code, study good competitors, and get obsessed with your client's world.
  • Overdeliver by being proactive: take ownership instead of blaming, solve the next problem early, and use unscalable care while you are small.
  • Keep the stack simple: Claude Code to build, GoHighLevel to run, Google Workspace to organize, Commas to get paid.

Set up your stack: Commas, GoHighLevel, Google Workspace. The checklist has the order and the links.

Copy the 48-hour sequence into your notes. Run it on your next client, even the free ones.
3
Create the WhatsApp group with your client today, and calendar-block the Sunday report. Narrate the work.
4
Buy or borrow ONE book about your niche this week. Become the obsessed person.

title: 9. Make It Inevitable
html:
Chapter Nine
Make It Inevitable
As long as you do not quit, you are still in the game. This chapter makes sure you never quit.

We are at the end, and I want to make sure of one thing. That you do not fail. You have come a long way. You understand marketing, sales, delivery, how to find good problems, and how to run a business. I have shown you it works, for me and for my students. So here is how you make winning inevitable, starting with a few non-negotiables. These are mine. Make them yours.

The non-negotiables

Family always comes first. I have gone down the rabbit hole of working and working and forgetting the people I was doing it all for. Do not. You miss things you cannot get back, and no amount of money is worth it. I would rather a goal take a year longer than lose the time with the people I love.

Train 3 to 4 times a week, minimum. Gym, martial arts, running, football, anything. Get 8 to 10,000 steps a day. I played football at a high level, but I also once locked myself in my room for two straight months building my agency. It was horrible. You burn out, you disconnect from the world, you gain weight, your knees hurt, you forget how to talk to people. Take care of your health and your relationships. They are the two most important things you have.

Be intentional with your time. When you work, work. When you rest, rest. Do not scroll and half-work, and do not answer business texts on vacation.

Two people do the same activity. The one who is fully present finishes it completely and gets a better result. The one splitting attention leaves it half done. When you work, you get more done. When you are with family, they feel you are there. When you rest, you actually recover. Working 24/7 is not a flex. That is not why you started a business.

Start living now

This one makes me angry, because I got it wrong for years. You have a dream life in your head. Wake up at 8, surf, learn Spanish, do your work, spend time with the people you love. You think you have to hit $10,000 a month first to live it. You do not.

Surfing is nearly free, rent a board and jump in the sea. Spanish is free, download Duolingo. Working is free. Time with your family is free. So live your dream life now. Do not wait. Yes, working 12 hours a day is more hours than 6 to 8. But if you work 6 to 8 hours fully and also live fulfilled, maybe it takes six months longer to hit your number, and in those months you were happy, healthy, you learned to surf, you got fluent in Spanish, and you built stronger relationships. When I postponed my whole life to grind, I just resented it and delayed my goals anyway, because I kept asking "why am I even doing this?" You can live 70 to 90% of your dream life today, for almost nothing. So live it.

Stickability

Here is the one that decides everything. Stick to your business for three years. Same model, same niche, same problem. Do not switch left and right. I did that for two years, trading, crypto, all the stuff from chapter one, and I got nowhere. Then I stuck with my lead generation agency for three years and scaled it past $20,000 a month by the time I was 19 to 21. It works if you stick.

You will be tempted to switch. Someone will suggest you sell a course. Do not, that is a completely different business, and you should never sell a course before you have real proof. Being a mentor was my dream for years, but I had to build a whole business and help dozens of owners first to earn the right to do it.

And you will face problems. Accounts get banned. Clients leave. Disputes happen. Someone leaves a bad review. I do not know a single 6 or 7 figure entrepreneur who has not been through all of it. It is part of the game. And because I promised you an anti-guru book, let me prove that sentence with the worst week of my business life, instead of pretending success is a straight line.

The $12,000 message

This did not happen when I was a beginner. I want that on the record before I tell it, because gurus love pretending problems are a beginner phase you graduate out of. This happened later, when the business was already working, when I had a track record, systems, happy clients. I thought weeks like this were behind me.

Then I opened my phone and the money was moving the wrong way. A client had filed chargebacks. Not a refund request, not an angry email I could answer. Chargebacks, through the bank, pulling back $12,000. Money I had earned. Money that, in my head, was already part of my life. Twelve thousand dollars, exiting, while I stood there reading the notification like it was written in a language I did not speak.

I will be honest about what the first hours felt like, because you might meet a version of this week yourself. It was not just the money. It was the unfairness of it, the story in my head screaming that I had delivered, that this was theft with paperwork. The devil from Chapter 3 came back with a megaphone: "This is why you cannot have nice things. Burn it down. Quit. Or at least go to war with this client and make it ugly." And underneath the anger, quieter and worse: "maybe everything you built is this fragile."

Here is what I actually did, and I give it to you as a protocol for your own worst week. First, I did not act for 24 hours. No angry messages, no decisions, nothing done in the heat. Second, I separated the two fights: the formal one, which is fought with paperwork, invoices, contracts, and delivery records through the dispute process, calmly and completely. And the internal one, which is the only fight that can actually end your business. A chargeback takes money. Only quitting takes the business. Third, I ran the accountability question from this book, the one I run on everything: "what could I have done to prevent this?" Not because the client was right, but because that question is the only one that pays. Clearer agreements, tighter invoicing, expectations in writing, earlier honest conversations when something feels off. Every answer became a system the next week.

And then I went back to work. Delivered for the clients I had, sent the outreach, ran the calls, with $12,000 less and one very loud lesson more. The business survived. It more than survived. And I learned the thing I most want to hand you: problems do not stop when you get good. They scale with you. Beginner you loses a $600 client. Later you meets a $12,000 chargeback. The size changes, the question never does: do you solve it and keep building, or do you let one brutal week erase three years of work? Stickability is not for the smooth months. Nobody needs it then.

The blame-yourself exercise, live

Since the accountability question is the engine of that protocol, let me show it working on a normal-sized problem, the kind you will meet in month one, because this exercise is the single fastest way I know to become the person clients never leave.

I had a client whose ads needed his face. Real footage, him talking. And he would not film. Weeks passed. Reminders got polite nods and no videos. The reactive move was sitting right there, and it even felt fair: "I cannot do my job because the client will not do his part." True, comfortable, and completely useless. His results would tank, and "it was his fault" would not save the case study or the contract.

So instead I sat down with the question: what could I have done to make this impossible to fail? And the answers were embarrassing, because there were so many. He was not lazy. He was a busy owner staring at a camera with no idea what to say. So I removed every gram of effort between him and the footage. I wrote the exact scripts, word for word, so there was nothing to think up. I sent a one-page iPhone guide: where to stand, which camera, how close, one take is fine. I made a shared drop folder so sending the clips took one tap. I set up daily reminders so remembering was my job, not his. And we agreed a deadline together, on a call, his words, his calendar.

The videos arrived that week. Every one of them. Nothing about the client changed. Everything about the system around him changed, because I stopped waiting to be right and started making it effortless to succeed. That is the whole exercise: when anything goes wrong, anything, you get one useless question and one paying one. "Whose fault is it?" pays nothing. "What could I have done?" pays forever. Run it on every problem for a year and watch what happens to your business.

So yes, you will face problems, at every level, forever. We are entrepreneurs. The one thing we are good at is solving problems. Do not run from them, especially when you most feel like running, when you want to switch niche or bolt on a random new service until you have 17 services you cannot run. Stick with what you built. Improve it, get feedback, iterate. But do not change directions.

Think of baking bread. The recipe is good, the ingredients are good. You put it in the oven, and it needs 15 minutes. After 2 minutes you get angry it is not done, so you pull it out, add things, remove things, put it back, and repeat. It never becomes bread. There was nothing wrong with it. You were just impatient. Your business is the same. Sometimes it is not wrong, it just needs time in the oven. Be patient. And how do you stay patient? By living your life while it bakes.

You are not getting graded. This is not school.

Read that twice, because school trained you wrong for this game. In school, a failed test went on your record. Red ink, permanent, everyone saw it. So your brain learned that mistakes are final and visible, and it still flinches like they are. But out here, nobody is keeping your record. A cold call that goes badly is not written anywhere. A campaign that dies gets deleted and replaced by Tuesday. The only thing that ever gets graded is whether you were still in the game when it clicked. So take the swing. There is no permanent record. There is only the next attempt.

The whole method, in four steps

Here is everything you learned, on one page.

1. Pick a problem with lopsided demand and supply. 2. Solve and package it into a Hat Trick Offer, using AI. 3. Make people know you exist, every single day. 4. Deliver a great service, every single day. Steps one and two you revisit only 1 to 3 times a year, reevaluating the problem and refreshing your offer. Steps three and four are daily. That is the whole business.

When you feel lost: Market, Close, or Deliver

There are only three things to do in your business: market, close, and deliver. If you are not doing one of those, you are on silly stuff. The priority runs from the bottom up. Deliver for the clients who already paid you, first, always. Then close the deals already on your calendar, the low-hanging fruit. Then market to get more people in. Do all three daily. Whenever you feel lost, ask one question: right now, am I marketing, closing, or delivering? Then go do one of them.

The Volume Law

If you want faster results, the answer is simple. Do more. A lot more. And I want to give you the law that runs it, because once you see it, you stop praying for luck.

The Volume Law: enough swings make luck irrelevant.

Look at the two figures in that picture. The one sending 200 emails needs luck. He needs the right owner to open the right message in the right mood, and if it does not happen, he learns almost nothing and calls the method broken. The one sending 10,000 does not need luck at all. Somewhere in 10,000 attempts, the yeses are mathematically waiting, and so are the lessons. If I send 10,000 cold emails and you send 200, who hits their goal first? Me, and not just because of the emails. More volume means more calls, more clients, more mistakes, and so faster learning and faster improvement, while you sit refreshing your inbox wondering why it is slow. Luck is just what low volume calls the odds.

So do not add a little. Multiply. Posting once a day? Post three times, AI makes it easy. Cold calling 150 a day? Get help and do far more. Whatever you think is a lot, the real number is 5 to 10 times that, within the limits of physics. I thought posting once a day was impressive until I posted seven times a day, and all I did was ask, "what would the version of me making $1 million a month do?" He would post seven times a day, on every platform. I had no real excuse not to, only excuses. So act like Version Two and run the law.

The Foundation Law: the slow way is the fast way

Hold on. I just told you to multiply your volume by ten, and at the start of this chapter I told you to train, sleep, and protect your family time. You are allowed to ask if I am contradicting myself. I am not, and the answer is the most important thing I have learned in five years.

The Volume Law is about the volume of the right actions. It is not permission to burn your life down. There is a version of "more" that compounds, and a version that destroys you, and they look identical for about six weeks. So let me show you both, from my own life.

What the fast way actually cost me

I always used to look for the fastest way. I sacrificed sleep. I sacrificed food, the gym, my health. I sacrificed family time and relationships. Whatever it took to reach the outcome sooner, I paid it, and I felt proud of paying it, because that is what the internet told me winners do.

Here is the bill. From sixteen, seventeen, all the way to twenty-one, when I went all in, I missed a normal upbringing. My friends were building memories with each other, and I was not there. I still cannot fully relate to what they talk about, and I cannot relate to a lot of people. That gets lonely. Money did not fix it, and the years are not coming back.

And here is the cruel joke: the grinding did not even work well. Twelve or fourteen hours a day is not twelve or fourteen hours of good work. The quality collapses. You make silly mistakes. You overlook things and forget things, because you are not functioning. It is not fun, and half the time it made no more money than a calm four hours would have.

Look closely at the advice I was following, because it does not survive one question. "Stop hanging out with your friends." Fine, I stopped. Now where is the money? Not being with my friends is not an action that earns anything. Nothing arrives because you subtracted your life. You make money by doing the things that make money, which is the entire subject of this book: solving problems.

What it looks like now

Today I do two to four hours a day of real, deep work. That is it. I have systems in place, and I have people in place. On Mondays my team and I get on a call, and instead of me nagging about slow progress, we laugh, we review last week, we set this week's goals, and we plan. Dead serious about the work, and enjoying it while we do it. Everyone keeps getting better. And it produces more than the fourteen-hour days ever did, because volume inside a system compounds, and volume inside chaos just tires you out.

The closer who took three months

Here is the clearest proof I have that the slow way is the fast way.

I hired a closer who had never closed a deal in his life. I interviewed him, liked how he showed up, liked his character, saw that he was willing to learn and willing to get uncomfortable, and I put him on a real sales call that same day. He did not close it. He did not close the next ones either. It took him about three months to close his first deal.

Run the fast-way math on that. Every one of those calls was a call I could have taken myself and closed. On paper, I lost money for three months. The fast move was obvious: fire him, hire a better closer, protect the numbers.

I believed in him instead. And look where that patience went. He is loyal in a way you cannot buy. He goes above and beyond without me ever asking. We are friends now, we travel together, and he is a cofounder of this university, helping our students for free, because he wants to. Tell me which transactional hire, closing perfectly from day one, ever turns into that. None of them. The slow way did not just get me a closer. It got me a partner. The fast way rents people. The slow way builds them.

Why slow is actually faster

Here is the part most people get wrong. Going fast without a foundation is not actually fast. You are just hoping something will work, but hope is not a strategy we want to play.

Picture the beginner who does everything as fast as humanly possible. He blasts a thousand cold calls with no system and no records, and he lands a client. Good. Now what? He does not know how to onboard them, so it stresses him. He has no repeatable process, so his delivery is improvised. And when you ask him the only question that matters, "what exactly did you do, and why did it work?", he cannot answer. He was just doing things. So he cannot do it again on purpose. He got a result he cannot repeat, and that is not a business. It is a lottery ticket that cashed once.

So build like a scientist instead. Here is what that actually means.

The Experiment Loop

When you run a science experiment, you do not start mixing things and hope. You write your hypothesis. You log every action you take. You run it. You read the result. Then you change one variable, and you run it again. Do that a few rounds and you are not guessing anymore. You know exactly which lever moved the outcome.

Your business is the same, and you already have every tool from this book. Your hypothesis is your offer and your avatar. Your log is the sheet from Chapter 6: every message, every call, every follow-up. Your result is the calls booked and the deals closed. Then you change one thing, the hook, the niche, the guarantee, the follow-up timing, and you run the next round. One variable at a time, or you will never know what worked.

Yes, this is slower up front. So take the trade with your eyes open. Maybe it takes you nine months to hit your first $10,000 month when a lucky sprint could have done it in four. But at month nine you are standing on something the sprinter does not have: you know exactly why it worked, so you can do it again on purpose. You have a system, a habit, a framework, and a business that does not collapse the moment you get tired. He has a story. You have a machine. And you still have your health, your friends, and your family, which he traded away for a five-month head start on a result he cannot reproduce.

That is the whole reason the slow way is the fast way. Not because slow is noble. Because the fast way keeps landing back at zero, and it bills you in health, relationships, and years to get there.

The Foundation Law: any speed that costs you your health, your people, or your ability to repeat the result is not speed. It is debt. Run the Volume Law inside the Foundation Law, and nothing can stop you.

The Real Why

Last thing. This one is the most important page in this book, and it is the one I got wrong for years. It cost me the only thing I actually regret, so I want to save you the same bill.

I ask every single person who gets on a call with me the same question: why do you want to make money online? And I hear the same three answers, almost word for word, every time.

  • "I want to travel."
  • "I want to be free."
  • "I want to be around like-minded people."

So I ask a second question. Why do you want that? And this is where it gets interesting, because the answer changes completely. It comes out quieter, and it always sounds like this:

  • "I want to take care of my mom."
  • "I want to get my parents out of that apartment."
  • "I want to give my family the life we never had."

Look at what just happened there. The first three answers were things social media told them to want. They are borrowed. The second set is the real one, and notice what every single one of them has in common: a person. Not a place, not a thing, not a lifestyle. A person they love.

The million-pound villa

I did the whole dream. I went to insane places. I stayed in a villa in Thailand worth about a million pounds. Eleven or twelve bedrooms, on top of a mountain, jungle all around it, views that do not look real. You could fit twenty-something people inside. You took stairs to get between rooms. I spent three to five thousand dollars in a single week to live there and do all the fun, stupid things you would expect.

Was it fun? Yes. And it felt empty. It felt fake. Not because of the villa, the villa was incredible. Because my family was not there. My siblings were not there. My closest friends were not there. I was surrounded by people I had met, like-minded people, and yes, I built real friendships with some of them, and they know who they are.

But I am sitting here writing this book, and where are they now? I do not even know which country most of them are in. That is not bitterness. It is just the honest arithmetic of that life.

Florianopolis

Then Brazil. I lived in Florianopolis, an island in Santa Catarina, for three months. On paper it was a perfect life. I would wake up and go to the gym or go out for a run. Come home, shower, sit down and work in a beautiful apartment with everything I wanted nearby. I could take the nice Ubers everywhere, eat at the most expensive restaurants, order the biggest meals on the menu, and never once check the price. There were people around almost every day. No limitations at all.

And that is exactly what did it. When there is nothing left to want, you find out what you actually wanted. I FaceTimed my parents every single day. And do you know what I was looking forward to? Breakfast with my mom and dad. A barbecue in the garden. Sitting in the living room with my family, doing nothing at all. Playing with my nieces, who I had not seen in three months, who are little and cute and growing up in rooms I was not in.

It is not fun to be in the Maldives if you are there alone.

The chain, all the way down

Run it from first principles and you cannot escape the answer. Why do you want to get in better shape? So you live longer. Why do you want to live longer? So you get more years with the people you love. Or so you look good for the person you love. Why do you want more money? To provide for the family you have, and the family you will have.

It is always relationships. The meaning of life is relationships, and I believe that with everything in me. Which makes the standard dream ironic to the point of stupidity: making money so you can travel away, for years, from the people you were making it for.

Do not misread me. Travel. Go be around ambitious people. It is genuinely valuable, and it changed me. Go do it for a month. Go do it for two or three. Live it, and then you have it, and it is yours forever. But the second mastermind, and the third, and the seventh, chasing the next expensive thing, living with strangers in a rotation of cities you will not remember, that is not a life. That is a treadmill with a view.

If I had to pick one thing I regret, that is it. I did the coolest things a person can do, without the people I actually love. Did it make me money sometimes? Yes. Did it build my network? Yes. Did it need a year and a half? Absolutely not. Two, three, four months would have given me everything it gave me.

What I actually want for you

So here is my honest recommendation, and it is not the one your feed will give you.

I would rather see you making $12,000 a month, consistently, sending $5,000 to $7,000 of it home to your parents and living well on the rest, than see you at $40,000 a month with your phone in your hand at every dinner. And read this part twice, because I am not telling you to think small: I want you rich. I want you to make a lot of money. I just want you to still be there when it arrives.

Picture it properly. Low cortisol. You are healthy, you train, you sleep. You sit through an entire barbecue with your family without checking your phone thirty-two times. You take two weeks away with your siblings, and you paid for it, and you do not have to work through it. You are running your experiments, one after another, building something that outlives you, and you are enjoying the years while you build it.

That is the life. Not the villa. My home is where my family is, and I had to fly across the world twice to learn a sentence my mother could have told me for free.

The deathbed math

One last thing, because somebody in your life is going to call this whole path risky, and I want you armed with how I actually think about that.

People measure risk from the wrong end of life. They stand at 20 and ask "what if the business fails this year?" Stand at the other end instead and ask the deathbed question: which path would I regret? Here is my honest answer, and I mean every word of it. If I had gone to university, gotten the degree, and done the nine to five for forty years, I would have hated my life. I would probably have ended it, and I genuinely mean that.

That is not a line for drama.It is why "risky" never scared me the way it was supposed to. The worst case of this path is a few embarrassing years and some lost savings, all of it recoverable. The worst case of the "safe" path, for a person built like me, and maybe like you, is an entire life spent as someone else. Only one of those is actually dangerous. So when the fear comes, and it will, do the deathbed math. Then get back to work.

And remember, as long as you do not quit, you are still in the game.

Summary

  • Non-negotiables: family first, train 3 to 4 times a week, and be fully present in whatever you are doing.
  • Live your dream life now. Most of it is free, and postponing it usually delays your goals, not speeds them.
  • Stick to one business, niche, and problem for three years. Problems scale with you, the $12,000 chargeback proved it, and the answer at every level is the same: solve it and keep building.
  • Run the blame-yourself exercise on every problem: "what could I have done?" is the only question that pays. Make success effortless for the people around you.
  • You are not getting graded. This is not school. Sometimes nothing is wrong, the bread just needs time in the oven.
  • The whole method: pick a problem, package a Hat Trick Offer, make people aware daily, deliver daily. When lost: deliver, then close, then market.
  • The Volume Law: enough swings make luck irrelevant. Whatever feels like a lot, the real number is 5 to 10 times that.
  • The Foundation Law: any speed that costs your health, your people, or your ability to repeat the result is not speed, it is debt. Run the Volume Law inside it. The fast way rents people, the slow way builds them.
  • Build like a scientist. The Experiment Loop: hypothesis, log everything, read the result, change one variable, run it again. Month nine with a machine beats month four with a story.
  • The Real Why is always relationships. Make a lot of money, and still be there when it arrives. My home is where my family is.
  • Do the deathbed math. The safe path is the risky one for people built like us.

title: The Dictionary and FAQ

Reference
The BDP Dictionary

Every named idea in this book, on one page. Use it to refresh fast, and to explain the method to someone else in their first five minutes.

BDP (Behavioral Demand Psychology)
The method this book teaches: find the problem, solve and package it, make them aware, fulfill. Built on how money actually works, so it does not expire like business models do.
Trust × Problem = Money
The master equation. The more someone trusts you and the bigger their problem, the more money you make. Bigger problem, bigger check, more trust required. (Chapter 4)
Version One / Version Two
V1 is the current you: runs from problems, lets doubt decide. V2 is the person who can make $10,000 a month. The whole game is crossing the gap. (Chapter 3)
Kill Version One
The 6-move protocol for crossing that gap: list the beliefs, find their origins, demolish and replace them, build the evidence bank, install the operating system, write the one-page document. (Chapter 3)
The Evidence Bank
A dated log of every kept promise and small win. Your brain believes receipts, not speeches, so you manufacture proof of the new identity daily. (Chapter 3)
The Dip
The motivation drop between day 4 and day 11 of any new push. Not a sign it stopped working. Shrink the day, never skip the day. (Chapter 3)
Denying Experience
A moment that contradicts a belief you hold. The only thing that actually breaks one, which is why you go and collect them on purpose instead of arguing with yourself. (Chapter 3)
Raise The Floor
You are the average of your best and worst weeks, so your worst week decides your life. Stop chasing bigger peaks and make your bad days less bad. (Chapter 3)
Hat Trick Offer
An offer that scores all three goals: gives them their dream outcome, removes what they hate, removes the risk with proof and a guarantee. They feel stupid saying no. (Chapters 5 and 6)
The 10% Rule
Price at 10% of the value you create. They win 9 times what they pay, which is why they say yes. Raise it as proof stacks. (Chapter 5)
The Beginner's Four
The four marketing methods a beginner runs: warm outreach, cold outreach, affiliates, and content. The other four ways come later. (Chapter 6)
The Lag Law
Today's inputs pay in 2 to 6 weeks. Judge days by inputs sent, and never stop sending on a good week. (Chapter 6)

Do I need to register a business before I start? What about taxes?

Rules differ by country, so here is the universal version. In most places you can legally earn your first money as an individual and register once real revenue exists, and registering is usually cheap and fast. Two habits keep you safe everywhere: keep every invoice and receipt from day one, and once money is actually flowing, pay a local accountant for one hour to set you up right. What you should not do is spend three weeks on legal setup before you have a single client. That is Version One hiding in paperwork. Get the client first.

How do I invoice a client for the first time?

An invoice is just a document that says: your name and details, their name and details, a date, an invoice number, what they bought, the amount, how to pay, and when payment is due. Free invoice generators online do it in five minutes, and Stripe creates and sends them for you. Send it right after the agreement, while the yes is warm. It feels official and scary the first time. It is a PDF. Send it.
